title: Count hook invocations at entry so starved and unparseable turns are measured, not declared residuals
description:
Follow-up to sr-count-prerecording-failures-73b6 (FuchsiaCave). After that fix, every hook failure that finishes inside its own total deadline records one typed unavailable row. A failure at the work deadline uses the new finalization clock (half the cleanup reserve). Two residuals are still unmeasured and are declared in docs/output-contract.md: (1) payloads that never parse, and (2) invocations starved past their own total deadline.

MEASURED on threadripperje, pinned build d103476d, replaying sr hook claude offline over the 40 most recent real transcripts three times (120 runs) at load 119-140: 7 runs left no row. All 7 overran the 3,000 ms total (3,141-6,244 ms; 6 with 'Runtime cleanup did not finish within the invocation deadline', 1 with 'Deadline exceeded during roster validation'). Every run inside the deadline recorded exactly one row. Before the fix, a single 40-run pass left 4 of 40 with no row, including in-deadline timeouts.

Under host starvation this is about 6% of turns, and they are exactly the turns an availability gate (.8.4, <=5% fallback) must count. Without a denominator for them, the gate can pass on a host where it should fail.

PROPOSAL (option 2 of the original bead): a bounded, owner-only, append-only invocation counter written at hook entry, before stdin is read. One fixed-size O_APPEND record (entry time and a random invocation token) goes to a small file beside the ledger, only when the ledger directory already exists and hook-level --no-ledger/--no-persist are not set. `sr stats` then reports hook invocations counted at entry against rows recorded, and the difference is the measured unrecorded count. This must: never block the hook (non-blocking open, the same deadline rules, and a failed append is silent); respect quota and retention like the ledger; use no network and write no credentials or content; and keep project config unable to enable it.

TESTS: a hook starved past its deadline (a tiny --timeout-ms plus slow stdin) still increments the entry counter; stats reports entry-counted minus recorded; --no-ledger and an absent ledger write nothing; an append failure never changes the hook's exit or stdout.
close_reason: Implemented and verified: entry counter + stats hook_entries + prune/clear alignment; unit 4/0, e2e 2/0, clippy clean, full 1340/3 (unrelated flakes, cass rerun 3/0)

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Caveat on the numbers above (FuchsiaCave): my replays used DEBUG builds (sr-a2dd3a5, d103476d). A peer's note says debug sr times out in retrieval where release does not, so 7/120 overstates the starvation residual an installed release binary would see. The mechanism finding (a run past its own total deadline leaves no row) stands; the rate needs re-measuring with a release build before it is quoted as the fleet residual.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: RELEASE RE-MEASUREMENT (AzureJaguar, 2026-09-22 23:41Z), as the caveat asks. Binary: release sr built by RCH from c8b6f8e's tree (freshness proven by strings, not mtime). Same shape as the original: sr hook claude offline over the 40 most recent real transcripts x3 = 120 runs; real HOME for the roster; XDG config/data/cache/state isolated in a scratch dir (no trusted config, no ledger, no key, no network); load average 106-145. Result: 0/120 over the 3,000 ms total; p50 141 ms, p95 161 ms, p99 169 ms, max 184 ms. So the 7/120 overruns were a debug-build artefact at this load, not the fleet residual for an installed release binary. (Correction to the attribution: the RCH note was about retrieving a 613 MB debug binary, not hook runtime; debug runtime is simply ~20x slower.) The mechanism finding stands: a run past its own deadline leaves no row, and networked runs spend most of the budget on the provider, so this counter is still how .8.4 gets a denominator. The measured offline starvation rate is just ~0 on release. Script: overrun.sh in AzureJaguar's session scratchpad; each run prints elapsed_ms and its first stderr line.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Implemented (AzureJaguar), built and tested in a clean export of origin/main c8b6f8e.
- src/storage/hook_entries.rs (new): at 'sr hook claude' entry (cli::run, before execute reads stdin), one fixed 54-byte record '{unix_ms:020} {32 hex}\n' is appended with a single O_APPEND write (O_NONBLOCK|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, mode 0600), only beside an existing ledger.sqlite3 in a real, owner-only ledger dir (--dir or the platform default, via storage_path), never under --no-ledger/--no-persist. Every failure is silent. Appends stop at 1 MiB (~19k entries). Only CLI flags and the ledger's existence decide it; project config has no say.
- sr stats: hook_entries {counted_since_unix_ms, counted_until_unix_ms, counted_at_entry, recorded, unrecorded, counter_full, unreadable_entries}. It compares entries with shadow/advisory-hook rows over [max(window start, oldest entry), as_of - 60 s], leaving out invocations that may still be running. It is absent when nothing was ever counted. Table output adds one section.
- sr ledger prune/clear apply the same cutoff to the counter atomically (rewrite + rename, owner-only) and report hook_entries_pruned / hook_entries_cleared (null means the counter could not be aligned).
- docs/output-contract.md: the 'unmeasured residual' paragraph now describes the measurement.
Tests: 4 unit tests (fixed-size owner-only records and windowing; nothing written without a ledger, in a shared dir, or through a symlink; full counter refuses the append and reports lower bounds; prune/clear with a torn record). E2E tests/hook_contract.rs hook_invocations_are_counted_at_entry_even_when_no_row_is_recorded, against the real binary: no counter before ledger init; an unparseable payload and a hook starved at --timeout-ms 50 with stdin held open are each counted; --no-ledger/--no-persist are not; a read-only counter leaves exit 0 and empty stdout; after backdating, stats counted=3, recorded=hook rows, unrecorded=3-rows; a fresh entry inside the settle window is not compared.
Gates: fmt clean; strict clippy clean; validate_public_contracts passed; RCH full --no-fail-fast 1340 passed / 3 failed / 10 ignored. The failures: 2 cass_session cases (rerun 3/0; subprocess tests, no hook or stats code) and the known sr-oj8g coordination flake.

title: ledger_snapshot_preserves_full_roster_and_rejects_overflow fails on a loaded machine because it writes 20,000 members inside the 3,000 ms default deadline
description:
FOUND 2026-09-21 (RoseCoyote) while gating sr-oufi. Recorded because I was misled by it twice in one
session, and so was the gate: a contract test whose verdict depends on machine load is a gate everyone
reads wrong.

WHAT HAPPENS. tests/ledger_schema_contract.rs::ledger_snapshot_preserves_full_roster_and_rejects_overflow
builds a 10,000-member roster snapshot, records it, reads it back, refuses a 10,001-member overflow, and
then records an equivalent snapshot with the members reversed and pretty-printed -- so two 10,000-member
JSON payloads are written within one ProcessInvocation. That invocation carries the product's default
deadline: 3,000 ms total with 200 ms reserved. When the box is busy the deadline expires mid-write and the
test panics on `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: `Cancelled`.

MEASURED, same binary, same tree, within a few minutes of each other:
  in the full suite (load ~130-156)  FAILED at line 289, Err(Cancelled)
  standalone (load ~70)             FAILED at line 322, Err(Cancelled), 4.11 s
  standalone x3 (load ~91)          PASSED, 1.15 s / 1.46 s / 1.44 s

So the work is normally ~1.2 s against a 2,800 ms usable budget, and contention is enough to triple it. The
failure line moves with which write loses the race, which is why it looks like two different bugs.

IT IS NOT A REGRESSION. The 10,000-member case arrived in 95e9e29; nothing recent touched
record_roster_snapshot. I checked this specifically because it first appeared in a gate run for an
unrelated change of mine, and a load flake that lands in someone's gate output looks exactly like a defect
they caused.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE NOISE. The test's PURPOSE is to prove a full 10,000-member roster survives a
round trip and that order and formatting do not create different evidence. That purpose is intact. What it
also does, silently, is assert that two maximal snapshot writes fit in the default deadline on whatever
machine happens to run it -- a performance claim nobody wrote down and nobody wants. AGENTS.md is explicit
that performance targets are targets until measured, and this is not how to measure one.

OPTIONS, in the order I would consider them:
  (a) Give the test its own explicit, generous deadline, so the deadline is a declared part of the case
      rather than an accident of the default. Keeps the 10,000-member coverage exactly as it is.
  (b) Split it: one case proves the full roster round trip, another proves order/formatting equivalence, so
      one invocation carries one maximal write rather than two.
  (c) Keep the default deadline and assert the outcome is either success OR a clean Cancelled, which is
      honest but proves less.
(a) is the cheapest and loses nothing. (b) is the tidiest. (c) I would not do, because a test that accepts
its own timeout accepts anything.

If the fleet's build contention is itself the thing to fix, that is a separate matter -- but the test should
not be the instrument that reports it.

TEST REQUIRED. Whatever the fix, the case must still fail if a 10,000-member snapshot is truncated or
reordered into different evidence: the point is the roster fidelity, and an explicit deadline must not
become a way to pass by not finishing.
close_reason: Independently verified (FuchsiaCave) at origin/main f41f133: 02a658d is an ancestor. Option (a): the case uses an explicit 60 s generous_invocation() rather than the default 3 s. The fidelity properties are intact: the stored members_json must have length 10,000; a 10,001 overflow is refused; the reversed, pretty-printed equivalent under the same snapshot must record without conflict; every write unwraps, so not finishing still fails. Passed in my full local suite at load 168->123.

comments.author: RoseCoyote
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED and PUBLISHED as 02a658d. Not closing it: I filed it and I fixed it, so someone else should.

The case now builds its invocation with an explicit 60 s deadline instead of inheriting the product's
3,000 ms. Sixty seconds is not a performance target; it is far enough above the real cost (~1.2 s of
work) that contention cannot reach it, so the assertions decide the outcome rather than the machine.
The deadline is the only thing relaxed -- every roster-fidelity assertion is untouched, so the case
still fails if a 10,000-member snapshot is truncated, reordered into different evidence, or if the
10,001-member overflow is accepted.

EVIDENCE: cargo test --locked --test ledger_schema_contract -> 14 passed / 0 failed in 3.04 s.
cargo fmt --check clean, clippy --all-targets -D warnings clean.

NO PLANTED NEGATIVE IS POSSIBLE HERE, and I would rather say so than dress something up. The defect
was that the verdict depended on machine load; the fix removes that dependence. Reverting the fix does
not reliably reproduce the failure -- that is precisely the property being removed. What I have instead
is the measurement that motivated it, from earlier today on the same binary and tree:

    in a full suite at load ~130-156   FAILED, Err(Cancelled) at line 289
    standalone at load ~70            FAILED, Err(Cancelled) at line 322, 4.11 s
    standalone x3 at load ~91         PASSED at 1.15 s / 1.46 s / 1.44 s

Same work, ~1.2 s against a 2,800 ms usable budget, tripled by contention. The failure line moving
between 289 and 322 is the same defect wearing two faces, which is part of why it reads as a code
problem.

WHAT A VERIFIER MIGHT REASONABLY OBJECT TO: 60 s is a magic number, and a case immune to its deadline
can hide a genuine performance regression in snapshot writing. I think that is the right trade here --
this case exists to prove what the store PRESERVES, and nothing measures write latency by asserting a
contract test finishes -- but if you want the latency watched, that wants its own measurement with a
declared denominator, not this test's silence.

comments.author: RoseCoyote
comments.text: WHOLE-SUITE CONFIRMATION at main 02a658d, which carries every change I landed today: `cargo test --locked --no-fail-fast` -> 133 reports | 1,265 passed | 0 FAILED | 10 ignored. For comparison, the same command earlier today at e4091d9's content was 133 reports | 1,262 passed | 1 failed, that failure being the regression I introduced and repaired in d7bf477. Main is green end to end with sr-oufi, the joint adoption case, sr-mdng, sr-jgez + its follow-up, sr-488b, sr-83cc and sr-0i7u all present.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION (AzureJaguar, not the author) at origin/main bef5ebc (contains 02a658d); clean git-archive export, RCH fell back to local. The explicit 60 s test deadline is at tests/ledger_schema_contract.rs:485. The author noted no planted negative exists for load dependence, so I tested the property the bead says must survive the relaxed deadline (roster fidelity), with two defects planted in validated_snapshot:
 (a) silent truncation (members.pop() after validation): the case FAILS at line 291, where the store refuses the write (so truncation is caught by the store's own consistency check before the test's 10,000-length assertion runs);
 (b) order normalization removed: the case FAILS at line 324 with RecordConflict, since the reversed, pretty-printed equivalent no longer encodes identically.
Restored: ledger_schema_contract 14/0 in 3.55 s at load average 120-142 (exactly the load that failed it before). It also passed in both of my full-suite runs today (1330/0/10 and 1331/0/10). The 60 s is a ceiling, not a latency claim; I agree write latency would need its own measurement.

title: Self-host sr in shadow mode on this repository to generate the operational and paired cohorts
notes:
REALITY CHECK 2026-09-21 (MagentaSquirrel), ambition round. The highest-leverage unexploited asset in
the project: SkillRanker's own development environment is its target environment, and nothing in the
backlog uses that.

THE OBSERVATION. This repository is a skill-rich workspace ($HOME/.claude/skills plus project skills)
worked continuously by multiple coding agents through Claude Code's UserPromptSubmit hook -- which is
exactly the integration `sr hook claude` implements, on exactly the harness the adapter targets.
Installing `sr` here in SHADOW mode would generate, as a byproduct of ordinary work and at near-zero
marginal cost, the two inputs the promotion gates assume into existence:

  - sr-roadmap-l1i.8.4 requires operational fallback at most 5% over at least 500 REPRESENTATIVE hook
    invocations, with outages and cold/cache/network strata. Nothing owns producing that traffic. A
    shadow hook on this repo produces several hundred real invocations per active day, with genuinely
    mixed cold/warm/cache strata and real provider behaviour including outages.
  - AGENTS.md and README both require measured latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99, cold startup and TLS,
    all-invocation fallback rates, memory, tokens, unknown usage) and explicitly forbid reporting only
    fast successful calls. The performance targets are labelled 'targets until measured'. Shadow traffic
    measures them on real rosters and real sessions rather than on a fixture.

Shadow mode is the right setting because it evaluates and records WITHOUT injecting advice, so it cannot
contaminate the agents' behaviour or the later relevance corpus. AGENTS.md permits this only with
explicit ledger initialisation and separate trusted network consent, and README states hooks default to
shadow; this bead does not change either default for anyone else.

THE SECOND, LARGER OPPORTUNITY. sr-roadmap-l1i.8.2 needs paired advice-enabled and baseline runs from
equivalent isolated snapshots, with identical permissions and budgets, randomised arm order and blinded
outcome review. This project's agents already work in isolated git worktrees on independent beads -- the
structural requirement for pairing is already satisfied by the development workflow. A paired arm
assignment over real bead work, with the outcome judged by someone who does not know the arm, is far
closer to reach than a purpose-built harm study. It is also the only design here that measures what the
product claims: whether the advice makes the work better.

WHAT MUST BE DECIDED, and decided before any traffic counts.
  1. Consent and privacy. This is real session content from real work. Shadow recording writes bounded
     local metadata, and capture of case bodies is separately opt-in; that boundary must be explicit
     before installation, not after. Absolute workspace paths, branch names and ledger identifiers stay
     local by default.
  2. Whether traffic from agents developing SkillRanker is REPRESENTATIVE. It is a real workload on a
     real harness, but it is one repository, one language, one unusually skill-dense library, and the
     sessions are agentic rather than human-paced. That is a declared population, not a general one,
     and the report must say so. This is the same discipline sr-uv2v demands of the relevance corpus.
  3. Provider budget. Shadow evaluation still calls Jev. Several hundred invocations a day is real
     spend, so the shared attempt allowance (sr-roadmap-l1i.7.4-.7.8, currently absent commands) is
     arguably a prerequisite rather than a parallel task -- which is an argument for raising the
     allowance work's priority, and a dependency worth recording.
  4. The blinding mechanism for the paired arm, since the obvious reviewer is another agent in the same
     fleet and 'independent' has to mean something concrete.

WHY THIS IS NOT CIRCULAR. Using the project's own environment for OPERATIONAL evidence -- fallback
rates, latencies, cache strata -- is sound: those measure the software's behaviour, not its judgement.
Using it for RELEVANCE labels would be circular if the labeller were the agent that received the advice,
which is precisely why shadow mode and blinded review matter. The distinction AGENTS.md draws between
adoption telemetry and independently judged usefulness is the line to hold.

RELATIONSHIP TO EXISTING WORK. Feeds sr-roadmap-l1i.8.4 (operational cohort), .7.12 (latency and
fallback), .8.2 and .8.3 (paired harm cohort). Companion to sr-uv2v, which owns the relevance corpus.
Depends in practice on .7.4-.7.8 for the shared allowance, and on .7.11 for hook qualification if the
trial ever moves beyond shadow. Does not change the shipped default, which stays shadow.

EXIT EVIDENCE. A declared population statement; ledger and consent boundaries recorded before
installation; at least 500 real shadow invocations with per-stratum fallback rates and p50/p95/p99
including cold startup and TLS; and a note stating plainly which gates this traffic can and cannot
satisfy. Traffic volume alone is not the deliverable.

REFINEMENT 1. Missing a rollback and coordination requirement, which matters because this installs a
hook into a workspace other agents are actively using.

Before installation: verify `sr uninstall-hook claude --apply` restores the prior settings exactly on
this machine, with the managed entry removed and unrelated settings preserved, and keep the backup path
recorded. Announce the change to the fleet through Agent Mail with the revision installed and the
uninstall command, because a hook firing on every prompt is a change to every agent's environment, not
just the installer's. AGENTS.md's coordination rules apply: unexpected tree changes are peer work, and a
hook is a shared-environment change of the same kind.

Also: install at a known-good revision and record it. A shadow hook running a build with a ranking
defect would produce operational evidence for a version nobody intends to ship, and the traffic would
have to be discarded. Pin the revision in the population statement.

REFINEMENT 2. Quantify the provider spend before installing, and decide the sampling question explicitly.

A shadow hook fires on every user prompt across every agent in this repository. At two logical requests
per invocation that is real money per active day, and the shared attempt allowance that would bound it
(.7.4-.7.8) does not exist yet. Estimate the daily invocation count from actual recent activity before
installing, not after.

If the estimate is unaffordable, sampling is the honest lever: run the shadow hook on a fixed fraction of
prompts chosen independently of anything about the prompt. An operational fallback RATE measured over an
outcome-independent sample is still a valid estimate of the rate, which is what .8.4 gates on -- unlike
relevance, where sampling interacts with case selection. State the fraction and the independence argument
in the population statement, and record that latency percentiles from a sampled stream describe the
sampled stream.

What must not happen is installing it, discovering the cost, and quietly reducing coverage afterwards;
that produces traffic whose population nobody can describe.

REFINEMENT 3, composition with sr-uv2v. Shadow traffic is not only operational evidence; it is the
cheapest source of the real sessions and rosters that the relevance corpus needs, and that raises this
bead's value well above the .8.4 gate it was filed for.

See sr-uv2v for the non-circularity argument. In short: take the session and roster from shadow traffic,
take the label from an independent adjudicator who never sees the recommendation. Shadow mode is what
makes that sound, because no advice was injected and no agent behaviour was influenced by the thing under
evaluation. If advisory mode is ever enabled here, that property is lost and the traffic stops being
usable for relevance labelling -- which is a reason to keep this deployment in shadow longer than a
feature-completion instinct would suggest.

Record retention accordingly: the sessions worth keeping as candidate corpus cases are a privacy artefact
with their own consent boundary, distinct from the bounded operational metadata that .8.4 needs. Do not
conflate the two retention decisions.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Execution correction from PurpleFrog: current fleet shares main; it does not establish isolated equivalent worktrees or independent paired experiments. Before counting any paired outcome, create and verify equivalent isolated snapshots and bound external effects/permissions per paired-cohort contract. Shadow traffic alone supplies operational/context evidence, not counterfactual benefit. Several hundred prompts/day and near-zero marginal cost are estimates in the original notes, not measured evidence; measure actual population and budget before enabling.

comments.author: RoseCoyote
comments.text:
MEASUREMENT, not a decision. I said I would not install a hook into a workspace other agents are using
without authorization, and I have not. What I can do unilaterally is replace the unknowns with numbers,
so the decision is a judgement about adjudication capacity rather than a guess about spend.

HOW MANY TIMES WOULD THE HOOK FIRE? Counted from the real Claude Code transcripts for this workspace
(~/.claude/projects/-data-projects-skillranker, 2 transcripts, 35,172 records), counting records that a
UserPromptSubmit hook actually fires on: type "user", not isMeta, not isCompactSummary, and not a
tool_result envelope.

    2026-09-17: 31    2026-09-18:  8    2026-09-19: 21
    2026-09-20:  6    2026-09-21: 30    TOTAL 96 over 5 active days, mean 19/day

CAVEAT ON THAT NUMBER, and it matters: only ONE Claude Code project directory exists for this repository,
so this counts Claude Code sessions whose cwd was /data/projects/skillranker. The codex, grok, omp and
antigravity agents in this fleet have no verified hook contract (AGENTS.md forbids claiming one from a
guessed equivalent), so they contribute nothing to this and their turns are NOT in the 19. If more Claude
Code agents join, the rate scales with them roughly linearly.

WHAT WOULD IT SPEND? At the per-rank cost this project has actually measured -- 2 logical requests and
about 275 known tokens for a ranked decision -- 19 turns/day is roughly:

    ~38 provider requests/day, ~5,200 known tokens/day
    ~1,140 requests and ~157,000 known tokens over a 30-day collection window

That is small enough that spend is not the reason to hesitate. Two honest qualifications: unknown usage is
real (AGENTS.md: an attempt without a response can still incur cost), and cache hits reduce it, so treat
these as an upper-ish bound on requests and a rough figure on tokens.

WHAT WOULD IT YIELD? ~570 candidate moments in 30 days at the current rate. Compare .8.8's gate of at
least 300 ADJUDICATED primary cases. Raw moments are therefore NOT the binding constraint -- a month of
ordinary work produces nearly twice the volume, and not every moment is a primary case. The binding
constraint is adjudication, which is sr-uv2v and needs a human decision about who labels and against what
rubric.

SO THE DECISION IN FRONT OF THE OWNER IS: authorise ~38 provider requests/day in shadow mode against this
repository for a month, accept a bounded per-turn latency on each Claude Code prompt (the hook's own
deadline, default 3,000 ms total with 200 ms reserved), in exchange for ~570 real moments with real
rosters. Shadow mode injects no advice, so agents' behaviour is not steered and the sessions stay usable
as evidence. Rollback is uninstalling the managed hook entry, which `sr uninstall-hook` previews before
applying.

WHAT I STILL WILL NOT DO WITHOUT A YES: install it. It changes an environment other agents are working in
and it spends real money against the maintainer's key. Announcing first was already required by this bead;
I would also want the announcement to name the exact settings entry and the rollback command.

comments.author: RoseCoyote
comments.text:
SECOND MEASUREMENT, zero spend, and it revises my own earlier figure downward.

My first comment measured how OFTEN the hook would fire (19 turns per active day) and inferred spend from
the per-rank cost. What nobody had measured is what happens BEFORE the provider: whether a real moment in
this workspace even produces a well-formed request. So I measured it with `--dry-run`, which the contract
defines as having no network or persistence effects -- ledger disabled, cache disabled, runtime state
disabled, network blocked -- against real turns from this workspace's own transcripts.

METHOD. 38,761 records, 97 submitted turns. Sampled 20 with seed 20260921 (a recorded seed proves
reproducibility, not randomness -- AGENTS.md). For each, wrote a transcript slice ENDING at that turn so
the turn is the current request, then ran
`sr rank --transcript SLICE --harness claude_code --dry-run --json`. No transcript content was printed or
retained; only the aggregates below.

RESULT at the product's own window (2,000 records / 2 MiB):
  14 of 20 (70%)  produce a well-formed wide request
   6 of 20 (30%)  refuse locally, exit 7, kind insufficient-context: "The request continues a task whose
                  instruction is not in the [window]" -- the essential-context check doing its job, at
                  zero spend
  wide request      median 46.1 KB, range 45.6-48.5 KB, against the 96 KiB serialized bound
  eligible          205 candidates from a 210-skill roster, so UNDER the 254-real-skill cap: no lexical
                    prefilter is exercised at this roster size
  local half        median 429 ms, max 525 ms, leaving roughly 2.4 s of the 3,000 ms deadline for the
                    provider
  trimming          description_cap 160, dropped_messages 0, omitted_description_scalars 11,992,
                    redactions 0 on the sampled moment

REVISED SPEND, which is lower than what I told you before: 19 turns/day x 0.70 reaching the provider is
about 13 provider-bound turns/day, so roughly 26 requests/day rather than 38, and proportionally fewer
tokens. My earlier number assumed every turn reaches the wire; 30% of them do not get that far.

TWO CORRECTIONS I MADE TO MY OWN HARNESS, recorded because each one initially looked like a product
finding and was not:
  - First run: every moment refused with exit 5, "No skills in the observed roster could be admitted
    (source-not-enumerated)". Cause: I pointed HOME at a sandbox with no skills. The real home has 210.
  - Second run: 12 of 20 refused with insufficient-context and I nearly reported 60%. Cause: I sliced
    400 records, a window TIGHTER than the product's own 2,000. Matching the real bound moved it to 6 of
    20. A measurement of a window I invented is not a measurement of the product.

WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SETTLE. It settles that a real moment here produces a well-formed, bounded,
un-redacted-secret request about 70% of the time, that the roster fits under the option cap, and that the
local half leaves the provider most of the deadline. It settles nothing about provider latency or answer
quality -- `--dry-run` never calls out, which is exactly why it was safe to run unauthorised. It is also
one agent's sessions, so the rate is this workspace's, not the fleet's.

The install itself still needs a yes, and still spends real money against the maintainer's key.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
The self-hosting deployment is PARTIALLY LIVE on threadripperje already, and measurably producing
nothing. Here is the exact state and the exact remaining checklist, measured rather than assumed, so
whoever authorises the spend is deciding with the full picture.

WHAT IS ALREADY IN PLACE:
- The hook is installed in `~/.claude/settings.json` as a `UserPromptSubmit` entry,
  `"/home/ubuntu/.local/bin/sr hook claude"`, `"timeout": 4`. The outer timeout correctly exceeds the
  3,000 ms internal deadline, which is sr-83cc's fix in a real installation.
- The ledger exists at `~/.local/share/sr/ledger.sqlite3`, schema initialised.

WHAT IT HAS PRODUCED, from `sr stats --json` against that real ledger:

    total_evaluated: 4     emitted_suggestions: 0     operational_failures: 3
    by_channel: [{"channel": "cli", ...}]      <- zero shadow-channel turns

Four turns, none from the hook, no suggestions, three operational failures. As an operational cohort
this is empty, and as a relevance signal it is nothing at all.

BLOCKER 1, filed as sr-t034 and already fixed in unpushed peer work. `sr hook claude` refuses every real
Claude transcript ("corrupt transcript JSON record") because a thinking-only assistant record and a
`system` record with no `message` are classified Corrupt rather than Unmodeled. Because a
pre-publication hook failure must emit empty stdout and exit zero, the hook has been failing silently on
every prompt. ProudBison's 40781b4/fa8976f/89d8488 fix it; I verified 6/0 against their tree versus 3/3
at origin/main. Needs pushing.

BLOCKER 2, which fixing sr-t034 does NOT remove, and which is the non-obvious one.
**`TYPESAFE_API_KEY` is absent from the Claude process environment on this machine.** I checked presence
only, never the value. A hook is launched by the already-running agent process and inherits ITS
environment, not the environment of whatever shell exported the key afterwards. So exporting the
credential in a terminal, or sourcing `.env` before running `sr` by hand, does nothing for the hook. The
key has to be present in the environment of the Claude process at the moment it starts. Until it is,
every hook turn will be recorded as an operational failure rather than a ranking, and the cohort will
grow without acquiring a single relevance observation.

BLOCKER 3. Network consent. docs/config-contract.md is explicit: "Network consent comes only from
`--allow-network` or trusted `network.enabled`." The installed hook entry passes no flags and cannot, so
a shadow deployment that actually calls Jev needs trusted user config `network.enabled = true`. Project
config cannot grant it -- the contract marks that layer forbidden for this key -- so it is a deliberate
user-level decision, which is the correct design and also means it will not happen by accident.

SO THE ORDER IS: push sr-t034's fix, put the credential in the agent process's environment, set trusted
`network.enabled`. After that the hook produces real rankings on real prompts and this bead starts
generating the cohort it exists for.

THE PART ONLY A HUMAN CAN DECIDE, stated plainly: steps 2 and 3 together mean a live Jev request on every
prompt submission in every session on this machine, with real cost, against real session content.
AGENTS.md is explicit that a loaded credential is not permission to send session content and that
recorded shadow trials require separate trusted network consent. Nothing in this comment should be read
as authorising that; it is the checklist for when someone does.

One measurement that bears on the cost question, from sr-t034's investigation: this session's transcript
is 80 MB and 41,054 records. The observation path reads a bounded tail, but sr-jgez and its boundary
repair exist precisely because long sessions stress that path, so a per-prompt hook on sessions this size
is the soak test nobody has run yet. Worth watching the hook's own latency against the 4-second outer
timeout once it is actually doing work.

title: Adopt relevance rubric v2: class from the acceptable set, near-miss as an agreement-defined attribute
description:
From the sr-uv2v diagnostic pilot (docs/relevance-corpus-contract.md §10, 9bd9a71). Outcome (c): rubric v1's near-miss set was not reproducible (11 of 18 cases disagreed between two blinded adjudicators, while acceptable sets agreed on 17 of 18). The positive stratum was degenerate: 0 of 18, because on a 205-skill roster every helpful case also has a tempting wrong skill. README's targets (>=150 positive, >=100 no-match, >=50 near-miss) cannot be met under v1.

ADOPT v2 (a new epoch; no v1 labels exist beyond the pilot):
(a) Class comes from the acceptable set alone: positive (non-empty) vs no-match (empty).
(b) Near-miss becomes an attribute of a positive case, counted only when two independent adjudicators name at least one near-miss skill in common. That makes it reproducible by construction; single-adjudicator near-miss lists are recorded but not counted.
(c) Three rubric clauses: partial fit under a constraint (acceptable when a permitted path exists and the constraint is stated); missing profile (judge only against what the request states); unstated environment (never assume it; judge the request as written).

CHANGE TOGETHER, and keep them consistent: docs/relevance-corpus-contract.md §3 and §6; README's promotion table (restate the strata as positive / no-match, with near-miss as an agreed-attribute subset of positive, keeping the counts' intent); scripts/validate_corpus.py (case_kind and strata keys, the agreed-near-miss check) and scripts/test_validate_corpus.py; anything in .8.1 that reads the strata.

title: Name the offending path and required mode when owner-only state permissions are refused
notes:
REALITY CHECK 2026-09-21 (MagentaSquirrel), refinement round 4. Small, first-contact usability defect
found by hitting it four times in a row while setting up a private workspace.

OBSERVED at origin/main 16743e9. `sr ledger init` in a directory whose ANCESTOR chain is group-writable:

    message: Failed to initialize ledger: cache path does not satisfy owner-only permissions
    hint   : Use sr --help; inspect trusted-user and project configuration.

The refusal itself is correct and good: the store must be owner-only and the product should not create
private state under a group-writable path. Two things about the diagnostic are not good.

1. It names neither the offending path nor the required mode. The failing component can be anywhere in
   the ancestor chain, and the message says 'cache path' while the command is initialising a LEDGER, so a
   reader cannot tell whether to look at the data directory, the cache directory, the explicit --dir, or
   a parent of any of them. It took four attempts to locate: chmod on $HOME, then on
   $HOME/.local/share, then passing an explicit --dir, and finally chmod on the grandparent that was
   actually at 0775.
2. The hint actively misdirects. 'Inspect trusted-user and project configuration' points at config files
   when the fix is `chmod 700` on a directory. A user who follows the hint reads the configuration
   contract and finds nothing, because configuration is not the problem.

Contrast with the case the product gets right, which is the model to copy: `sr stats` with no store
returns 'Ledger store is missing; run sr ledger init first'. The MESSAGE carries the next concrete step
even though the hint is generic. That is exactly the affordance the permission refusal lacks.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN ITS SIZE SUGGESTS. `sr ledger init` is step 6 of README's Quick Start and the
gateway to every P5 feature -- stats, observe, feedback, replay, eval all require a ready store. A user
whose home or state directory is group-writable (common on shared machines, containers, and CI images)
meets this as their FIRST interaction with local history, with a message that misdirects them. README
promises doctor 'names the next concrete step for a failed check'; this refusal should meet the same bar.

WHAT TO DO. Report the specific path that failed the check and the mode it needs, and replace the hint
with the action: something of the form 'cache path /x/y is mode 0775; owner-only state requires 0700 --
run chmod 700 /x/y'. Do not print the whole ancestor chain or anything about other users' paths, and do
not weaken the check itself. If several components fail, name the outermost one, since fixing that is
the first necessary step. `sr doctor` should surface the same diagnosis under its ledger readiness
check, which is where a user looks when setup fails.

TESTS REQUIRED.
- A group-writable ancestor produces a message naming THAT path and the required mode; assert on the path
  appearing in the message, which is the planted negative since today's message contains no path.
- The hint names the corrective action rather than configuration inspection.
- The refusal still happens: no test may make the permission check pass by relaxing it.
- `sr doctor` reports the same offending path under ledger readiness.
- An explicit `--dir` whose own mode is wrong names that directory rather than a platform path.

title: Response cache TTL can be extended by a clock rollback that stays after the receipt time
description: Reported by the 2026-09-23 review. src/cache/response.rs ~127 only rejects now < received_at, and the age is now - received. An NTP step back of 5 minutes at T+9 min makes a T entry fresh until T+15 min: a 900 s lifetime against the 600 s maximum. AGENTS.md: clock rollback cannot extend TTL. The storage prune (src/storage/mod.rs ~800) behaves the same way.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: Design note (AzureJaguar, 2026-09-24): a wall-clock high-water mark does not fix this; it freezes age during a rollback, and the real lifetime is still 15 min. The fix needs a boot-scoped monotonic receipt: store (boot_id from /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id, CLOCK_BOOTTIME ms from /proc/uptime) beside received_at_unix_ms, and use age = max(wall age, boottime_now - boottime_received) when the boot_id matches. On macOS or a different boot, fall back to wall age only. Blocker: read_stamp requires exact DDL and initialize() has no migration, so sr_cache_response columns mean CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION 4 plus a v3->v4 migration. Otherwise every deployed cache becomes IncompatibleSchema. Prune (storage/mod.rs ~800) needs the same age rule.

title: Diagnose concurrent runtime construction exhausting subprocess test budgets
description: During sr-dy6i default-parallel subprocess_contract run on vmi1153651, five existing tests failed in request_cx before spawning a child: 400ms invocation had already consumed718-852ms constructing the runtime. Two new1200ms bulk tests also exhausted budget; serial13/13 subprocess and full667/0/8 passed. Logs /data/tmp/sr-dy6i-focused.stderr; frozen9f076ef plus repair overlay301d1547232bfac5e4f0c5b81ce38888587135009e73c905337bf3fdafbf0187. Investigate actual setup contention/allocation and whether test harness can bound resource contention without hiding production startup latency. Preserve process-entry deadline semantics, existing cleanup/cancellation assertions and negative controls; do not report serial pass as parallel proof or merely increase limits until green. Establish revision-bound default-parallel negative and repaired evidence and log setup/send/cleanup timing without secrets.
notes:
Diagnosed, with measurements (CopperWren).

The title's hypothesis — that constructing the runtime is slow — is wrong. Measured
with the built binary on this 128-core host:

- idle, 12 runs of `sr capabilities --json` (debug build, whole process including
  clap and output): 11, 11, 11, 11, 11, 12, 12, 12, 12, 13, 14, 14 ms;
- confined to two CPUs with eight competing `sr` processes: 23, 11, 11 ms;
- confined to two CPUs with sixteen busy loops saturating both: 18, 16, 15 ms.

Runtime construction is single-digit milliseconds and CPU starvation alone does
not move it. `EntryClock::capture()` sets `started` to the call, not to process
start, so a long-lived test binary does not inherit elapsed time either.

The actual mechanism is the budget these tests choose. `tests/subprocess_contract.rs`
builds every invocation from `total = 400ms, cleanup = 200ms`, which leaves a
**200 ms work budget** that has to cover runtime construction, the test's own
filesystem setup, and the work under test. `ProcessInvocation::request_cx()`
returns `Err` the moment that budget is gone, which is why the five failures
landed in `request_cx` before any child was spawned — nothing had gone wrong with
subprocesses at all. `tests/storage_contract.rs:438` is tighter still at
`total = 60ms, cleanup = 20ms`, a 40 ms window, which is the case I saw fail on
vmi1227854. Two other tests share the shape: `tests/limits_contract.rs:249` and
`tests/roster_resolution.rs:693` at 20 ms.

For comparison, the product's own default is 3000 ms with a 200 ms reserve, about
seventy times the headroom. So this is test-design fragility under shared-worker
load, not a product deadline defect — but it is not harmless: a failure everyone
learns to ignore gave cover to a genuinely broken test for hours (sr-61j8), which
is exactly what happened in the run I was verifying.

Fixing the tests rather than the budgets: the property each case asserts is about
what happens once the window has expired, not about the window being 40 ms, so a
bounded retry that re-captures the clock when construction has already eaten the
budget preserves every assertion and removes the race. Where even a retry cannot
win, the case should report an unqualified environment rather than a failure.
close_reason: Diagnosis (CopperWren) confirmed and the remaining observed flake fixed (ProudBison): the recurring full-suite failure a_late_rerank_answer_is_never_published at rank_acceptance.rs:394 was the near-expiry-drain shape of the same design fragility -- a scenario returning ~80ms before expiry left no scheduleable drain window under load >100. Fix honors the bead's constraints (no production deadline change, no inflated scenario budgets, assertions and negative controls preserved): new ProcessInvocation::shutdown_within gives tests an explicit bounded drain; the helper uses the remaining budget when >=250ms and a fresh 1000ms window otherwise, so a wedged runtime still fails. Evidence: full suite 1318/1318/0 twice back-to-back, second run under load average ~81; rank_acceptance 56/56; clippy -D warnings clean; runtime.rs production shutdown() semantics untouched.

  tests/storage_contract.rs:438               retry ALREADY present, 16 attempts, 40 ms budget,

  tests/subprocess_contract.rs bulk_invocation()   THE GAP. No retry, and it is the other site the
                                              original report named: "Two new 1200ms bulk tests also
                                              exhausted budget."

WHY THAT ONE WAS MISSED, I think: 1,200 ms total against a 200 ms reserve leaves a 1,000 ms work budget,
five times the tighter case's, so it reads as having plenty of room. The measured construction delay in
the original report was 718-852 ms -- inside it.

panic wording as invocation() directly above it, so the file keeps one idiom rather than gaining a second.

comments.text:
Another data point for the root cause, with the numbers this time, from a whole-suite run I did for an
unrelated change.

`rank_acceptance::a_late_rerank_answer_is_never_published` failed in a `cargo test --locked
--no-fail-fast -j 4` run whose host five-minute load average was 103.88:

    owned runtime must shut down: startup 263 ms, returned at 1970 ms of 2000, 30 ms left,
    shutdown took 30 ms

The interesting number is the first one. **Startup alone consumed 263 ms of the 2,000 ms budget**, and
the assertion then missed by exactly zero: 30 ms left, 30 ms spent. The test is not marginal on its own
terms -- it passed 3/3 in isolation immediately afterwards at ~4.5 s each with load around 92 -- and the
same whole suite an hour earlier at a6f1ff0 had it passing with 0 failures. Nothing about the assertion
changed; what changed was how long the runtime took to come up.

Why I think this is your bead's shape rather than a separate flake: sr-5n0b is about concurrent runtime
construction exhausting subprocess budgets, and 263 ms to construct an owned runtime is the same
phenomenon measured from the other end. Under `-j 4` several test binaries construct Asupersync
runtimes simultaneously on a box already at load 100+, and construction time is what inflates. The
bridge plan's second executable-journey pass recorded this same case failing twice at load above 110
and then passing 3/3 in isolation, and named it the same shape as this bead; this adds the actual
startup figure to that observation.

If it helps the diagnosis: the failure is a *composite* of startup and shutdown against one deadline,
so a fix that only speeds up shutdown will not move it. The budget is consumed before the work begins.
Whatever bounds runtime construction under contention is the thing to find, which is what this bead
already says.

Not claiming this reproduces your root cause, and I am not claiming the suite is green on this host.
This is one measured instance offered as evidence, with the denominator stated: one failure in one run
of 138 reports, and 3/3 passing in isolation minutes later.

title: hook_installer_contract::reports_enterprise_read_only_restrictions cannot pass as root, so the RCH fleet suite is red
design:
## What happens

`tests/hook_installer_contract.rs::reports_enterprise_read_only_restrictions`
makes a settings directory mode 0500 and asserts the installer reports a
read-only restriction. Root ignores discretionary write permission, so the write
succeeds and the assertion fails. RCH workers run builds as root, so anyone who
runs the full suite through `rch exec` sees this as a failure that has nothing to
do with their change.

## Measured

- On worker vmi1227854 (root): the test fails inside a full-suite run.
- Locally as uid 1000 (ubuntu): `1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 9 filtered out`.

Same tree, same binary, both runs; the only difference is the effective uid.

## Why it matters beyond noise

A failure everyone learns to ignore is worse than a missing test: it trains
readers to discount the suite, and it hid a second real environmental failure in
the same run for me until I checked both by uid.

## Suggested shape, for whoever takes it

Mode bits cannot express "read-only" to root, so the property genuinely cannot be
established in that environment. Detect the effective uid and skip with an
explicit reason, so the case reports as unqualified rather than passing by
accident or failing by environment. An alternative is a real read-only mount,
which needs privileges the suite should not want. What it must not do is relax the
assertion so that root passes: that would delete the coverage rather than label it.
close_reason: Added nix::unistd::geteuid().is_root() early return in hook_installer_contract::reports_enterprise_read_only_restrictions since root bypasses POSIX DAC write permissions; verified via RCH on hz2

title: Shadow hook records one ledger event ever: event-0 collides and timestamps are monotonic, not unix
description:
Found by dogfooding the shadow hook that just landed in 5179ff3 (sr-roadmap-l1i.7.1), using the installed release binary from 90cd5da against a real Claude UserPromptSubmit payload. Two defects in ledger recording, both of which make the P5 observation ledger and the P6 shadow hook record almost nothing in production.

REPRODUCTION, exactly as run:
1. sr ledger init in a clean 0700 home (before this, the hook silently records nothing at all, because the ledger is ExistingOnly; that is defensible but undiscoverable).
2. Pipe a realistic payload three times: {"session_id":"aaaaaaaa-...","transcript_path":"<real jsonl>","cwd":"<workspace>","prompt":"My cargo tests are failing after the last refactor, please fix them.","hook_event_name":"UserPromptSubmit"} into: sr hook claude --shadow --allow-network
3. All three runs: exit 0, 0 bytes stdout, 0 bytes stderr, exactly as the quiet contract requires.
4. Ledger after three runs: ranking_events = 1 row, (event-0, shadow, ranked, prepared, created_at_unix_ms=41). ranking_candidates 2, roster_snapshots 1, provider_attempts 0, observations 0.

DEFECT 1: event_id is not unique per invocation, so only the first ranking is ever recorded.
src/pipeline.rs:3756 derives event_id from context.current_request.event_id and falls back to the literal "event-0". A real Claude UserPromptSubmit payload carries session_id, transcript_path, cwd, prompt and hook_event_name but NO prompt id, so src/context/overlay.rs:135 copies hook.prompt_id = None into the overlaid request, the fallback fires, and every hook invocation tries to insert event_id "event-0". ranking_events has event_id as PRIMARY KEY, so the second and later inserts conflict and the failure is swallowed as degraded observability. The result is one recorded event per ledger, for all sessions, forever. Every subsequent turn is invisible to observation, adoption denominators and evaluation.

DEFECT 2: created_at_unix_ms holds a monotonic offset from process start, not a unix timestamp.
src/pipeline.rs:3752 (roster snapshot) and src/pipeline.rs:3784 (ranking event) both use invocation.clock().now().as_millis(), which EntryClock defines as milliseconds since process entry. The observed value was 41. Every row is therefore dated 1970-01-01T00:00:00.041Z. That breaks retention and sr ledger prune --before TIME (which compares this column and would treat all history as ancient), any time-ordered analysis, and the frozen-time requirements of the replay artifact contract. This one is an unambiguous correctness bug with an unambiguous fix: use a wall clock, as the response cache and coordination leases already do.

PROPOSED FIX for defect 1, which is an identity decision rather than a typo, so it belongs to the ledger owner: derive the event id from the hook delivery when the harness supplies no prompt id, as a digest over session_id, the transcript state at hook time (its generation or last complete event id) and the prompt text. Two deliveries of the SAME turn, such as a retry, see the same transcript tail and the same prompt and therefore produce the same id, which satisfies 6.8s rule that a duplicate delivery must not generate another training example. A later turn sees a different tail because the previous turn is now recorded, so identical prompt text in two turns still yields distinct ids, which satisfies the standing rule that equal prompt text alone does not make two turns duplicates. Never fall back to a constant.

Filing rather than silently fixing both because defect 1 changes recorded identity semantics that 6.8 and 6.9 depend on. I am fixing defect 2 (the clock) directly, since there is no design choice in it.
close_reason: Derived deterministic hook event_id from session_id, last event_id, prior event count, and prompt text; replaced monotonic offset with wall-clock unix timestamp; plumbed ledger_dir through RankArgs; verified by tests/hook_contract.rs and full test suite

title: Install the Claude hook with an outer timeout strictly above the rank deadline
description:
REALITY CHECK 2026-09-21 (second executable-journey pass, HEAD a82abbb).

OBSERVED. `sr install-hook claude` previews a managed entry with "timeout": 3 (src/installer.rs:32, DEFAULT_HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS = 3). The internal ranking deadline defaults to 3,000 ms total with the final 200 ms reserved for output and cleanup, starting at process entry. Process startup (cold binary, TLS state, config reads) precedes the internal clock, so a 3 s harness timeout can kill sr BEFORE its own deadline fires — precisely during the 200 ms output reserve.

CONTRACT VIOLATED. README.md 'Agent Hooks': installation uses 'a harness timeout above the ranker's deadline'; README.md 'Performance': 'The Claude harness timeout is initially four seconds.' AGENTS.md: 'A later internal deadline change cannot exceed the installed outer timeout.' At defaults the outer timeout equals, not exceeds, the inner deadline, and it is 3 s where the docs say 4 s.

ACCEPTANCE. (1) DEFAULT_HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS strictly exceeds the default internal deadline plus measured worst-case startup (restore the documented 4 s, or update README/AGENTS if 3 s is deliberately chosen and proven safe). (2) install-hook refuses --timeout-secs values not strictly above the effective internal deadline with a named reason. (3) A regression test pins outer > inner at defaults. (4) Reinstall/upgrade path flags an existing managed entry whose timeout no longer satisfies the rule.

Found while auditing the hook boundary; no existing bead covers it (searched open/in-progress titles and notes for hook+timeout).
close_reason: Implemented and verified at 39c6d3b (origin/main). Two parallel fixes landed and were union-merged by the fleet: b83265b (this reviewer's: DEFAULT_HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS=4, min-timeout validation, installed_hook_budget_ms deriving the hook's internal clamp budget from the actual managed entry) and the origin/main side (check_hook_timeout/TimeoutTooTight/minimum_hook_timeout_secs). LIVE VERIFICATION at 39c6d3b: install-hook claude previews timeout: 4 (strictly above the 3000ms internal deadline + 1s startup reserve); --timeout-secs 3 refused exit 2 naming the required minimum 4 and the reason; SR_TIMEOUT_MS=10000 raises the requirement to 11 (contract test); hook with installed 10s entry and --timeout-ms 8000 is NOT clamped (budget derived from entry, not the old hardcoded 3000). Regression tests in tests/hook_installer_contract.rs (4 timeout tests incl. refusal and clamp-derivation) pass 14/14; storage 13/13. ACs met: default strictly above deadline; refusal names minimum; regression pinned; stale entries surface as Conflict on reinstall via classify_existing_entry timeout comparison.

title: Hook overlay is fatal on any transcript record over 256 KiB: one large tool_result silences the hook for that session
description:
FOUND 2026-09-22 (FuchsiaCave) by replaying HEAD a2dd3a5's `sr hook claude` (offline, no key, isolated ledger) over the 40 most recent real Claude transcripts on threadripperje: 35 got through context capture, 1 failed with `malformed-input: Claude prompt overlay failed: existing transcript file is malformed: transcript record exceeds byte limit`, and 4 were deadline cases (sr-73b6).

The failing session (-data-projects-jazz-chord-progression-editor-html/8a9b5d26..., 2,550 records) has two records over the 256 KiB per-record limit: records 2142 (541 KiB) and 2214 (529 KiB), both ordinary user `tool_result` records (large tool output), not malformed JSON.

CAUSE: src/context/overlay.rs (~line 290) maps `SkipKind::Oversize` to a fatal `malformed(...)`, on the principle that genuine malformation stays fatal because the overlay binds the authoritative prompt. An oversize record is not malformation. The JSONL reader already skips oversize lines and keeps their neighbours (jsonl_snapshot::oversize_complete_line_is_skipped_neighbors_kept). The overlay is stricter, so every hook turn in such a session fails until the big record leaves the 2,000-record tail. Large file reads make this common in real sessions.

DESIGN CONSTRAINT: simply dropping the record breaks lineage. Current transcripts chain parentUuid through every record (see 00c75b3), so a missing node can split the chain and turn this into ambiguous-branch. Options: (a) bounded extraction of uuid/parentUuid/sessionId from an oversize line, without a full parse beyond the bound, keeping it as a lineage pass-through node with its content marked omitted (context_quality partial); (b) keep the record fatal only when it is the prompt-bearing record itself. The 256 KiB bound must hold for any allocation made on its behalf.

TESTS: a real-shape transcript with a >256 KiB tool_result mid-branch gets through the overlay with the branch resolved and source_gaps/partial set; an oversize record that is the pending prompt's own record stays refused; a replay of the 8a9b5d26 shape records cache-miss offline rather than malformed-input.
close_reason: Duplicate of sr-xy2q, filed minutes before its fix landed (354f32b: oversized records keep lineage via an identity-only parse, a content-free placeholder, and Partial context). My replay evidence (the 8a9b5d26 session, records 2142/2214 at 541/529 KiB tool_result) matches its analysis.

title: Upgrade an attempted load to observed when its tool result arrives in a later ingestion pass
notes:
REALITY CHECK 2026-09-21 (MagentaSquirrel). Found while driving the documented adoption loop at
origin/main 16743e9 against the project's own TLS fixture, then reading observations rows directly.

OBSERVED, two runs that differ only in when the transcript was read.

A. Both records present before the first ingestion. A Claude transcript carrying a Skill tool_use
   and its tool_result, observed once:
       observations: [('loaded', 's_4e130c480f2994a0fc26', None)]
   This is the promised 'Observed successful load'. The state machine is right:
   src/context/tool.rs:445 maps ToolStatus::Succeeded with no error lines to
   LoadState::ObservedLoaded.

B. The records straddle an ingestion boundary. Observe once after the tool_use is written, then
   append the tool_result and observe again:
       observe #1 -> observations_recorded: 1, cursor_generation 2, state 'attempted'
       observe #2 -> observations_recorded: 1, cursor_generation 3, state STILL 'attempted'
   `sr stats` then reports observed_loads=0, attempted_loads=1, suggestion_adoption_rate=0.0 for a
   skill the agent did in fact load. The second pass cannot repair it because the cursor has already
   advanced past the tool_use, so the result arrives with nothing to associate against.

WHY IT MATTERS. This is not an exotic race. `sr observe` is documented as a periodic reconciliation
step and the hook runs once per user turn, so an ingestion landing between a tool_use and its result
is ordinary. Every such load is permanently recorded as an attempt. The consequence is a systematic
one-directional undercount of the headline adoption metric: README's 'Observed successful load' row,
suggestion_adoption_rate, observation_coverage, and the per-skill observed_loads column all read low,
and they read low precisely for the skills an agent actually used. Worse, the error is invisible from
the output: 'attempted' is a legitimate state, so nothing in the report distinguishes 'the agent tried
and we could not confirm' from 'we saw the try, then threw away the confirmation'.

This also interacts with usefulness measurement. AGENTS.md requires that 'A successful resolved load,
attempted load, unobservable load, and censored observation are different states' and that missing
events never become negative labels. An adoption denominator that silently loses successes will bias
any later comparison that uses adoption as a covariate, and it makes the honest caveat in
docs/output-contract.md ('observed adoption is not task success') sound like the only problem when
there is a second, mechanical one underneath.

WHAT TO DO. Allow a later pass to complete an observation it already recorded, rather than treating
the tool_use as consumed evidence. Two shapes are plausible and the choice needs deciding here, not
in review:
  (a) Keep a bounded pending-association window: when a tool_use is observed without a result, retain
      enough identity (tool_use id, skill id, event id) to upgrade the SAME observation row when the
      matching result is later read. The observation id already embeds the tool_use
      ('obs-<session>-<uuid>-<skill_id>'), so the row is addressable; only the upgrade is missing.
  (b) Defer the observation until the association is resolvable, leaving the cursor behind the
      tool_use. This is simpler but conflicts with AGENTS.md's 'Never advance the observation
      watermark across unread bytes' only in appearance -- it would instead hold the watermark, which
      risks an unbounded stall on a turn whose result never arrives.
(a) is preferred because it preserves forward progress and keeps the bounded-ingestion guarantee.
Whichever is chosen, an upgrade must be monotone: 'loaded' must never regress to 'attempted', and a
failed result must not upgrade anything.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MUST SURVIVE. Attribution to the latest eligible preceding emission in the same
agent/turn. Censoring of superseded recommendations. The bounded 8 MiB per-invocation ingestion cap.
Atomic commit of observations, loaded-state evidence and cursor advance under the expected cursor
generation. A path-only read still cannot prove a content version.

TESTS REQUIRED.
- Split ingestion: observe after the tool_use, append the result, observe again, and require the row
  to read 'loaded' with the same observation id. This case fails today and is the planted negative.
- Single-pass ingestion keeps working (regression guard for case A above).
- A failed or error tool_result leaves the state 'attempted' and never upgrades.
- An upgrade is monotone under repeated observes and does not double-count in
  observed_loads.
- `sr stats` reports observed_loads=1 and a non-zero adoption rate for the split-ingestion case,
  which is the user-visible property that is wrong today.
- A tool_use whose result never arrives stays 'attempted' and does not stall the cursor.

RELATIONSHIP TO EXISTING WORK. sr-roadmap-l1i.6.26 owns 'cursor CAS replay without skips' and the
observation lifecycle, but that clause is about not skipping unread bytes; this defect is the opposite
direction, where nothing is skipped and the association is nevertheless lost. sr-roadmap-l1i.6.13
consumes the resulting counts. Neither names this behavior, which is why it is tracked separately.

REFINEMENT 1. The first pass did not say what happens to ATTRIBUTION on upgrade, and getting that wrong
would be worse than the defect.

Attribution must stay bound to the emission that was current when the load was first observed. It must
NOT be recomputed at upgrade time. README specifies attribution to 'the latest eligible preceding
emission in the same agent/turn'; if a later `observe` recomputed it, a load first seen under emission
A could silently re-attribute to a newer emission B that the agent had not yet received when it loaded
the skill. That would invent adoption for B and erase it for A, which is a worse error than reporting
the load as merely attempted. So: upgrade the evidence state and the load timestamp, preserve
attributed_event_id exactly as first written, and add a test that a new emission arriving between the
tool_use and its result does not move the attribution.

Also unspecified: what `sr stats` should report while an observation is pending upgrade. It should
remain in attempted_loads and out of observed_loads -- the current behaviour -- because a pending
association is genuinely unconfirmed. The defect is that it stays there forever, not that it is there at
first.

REFINEMENT 2. The pending-association window needs a concrete bound, which 'bounded' did not supply.

An unbounded set of pending associations is a memory and storage leak in a long session, and it would
also let a stale tool_use upgrade against an unrelated later result. Specify both dimensions: a maximum
number of pending associations retained per session, and a maximum age or event distance after which a
pending association EXPIRES into a terminal attempted state and can no longer be upgraded. Expiry must be
recorded, not silent, so a reader can tell 'never confirmed' from 'confirmation arrived too late'.
Terminal attempted is the correct resting state for an expired pending association: it is what the
evidence supports.

The bound also has to respect the existing 8 MiB per-invocation ingestion cap, so pending state must be
counted against something, not kept off the books.

REFINEMENT 3, cross-bead. See the joint case recorded on sr-oufi: one end-to-end test covering rank ->
split-pass observe -> feedback-by-name -> `stats --by-skill`, requiring a single row with
top1_recommendations=1, observed_loads=1 and judged_useful=1. That single assertion is the real acceptance
for this pair; it fails today for two independent reasons and will keep failing if only one bead lands.
Whichever bead lands second owns adding it.

comments.author: RoseCoyote
comments.text:
DESIGN SETTLED BY READING THE CODE, and the bead's two refinements need correcting before anyone
implements them. The defect is real and reproduces exactly as recorded; the prescribed shape was wrong.

WHAT I FOUND, in order.

1. src/context/tool.rs is CORRECT within one pass: an invocation plus its result becomes
   LoadState::ObservedLoaded.
2. An orphan tool_result DOES become an AssociatedToolCall (invocation_event_id None), but
   resolve_tool(name, None) cannot identify the skill without the invocation's arguments, so a
   result-only pass emits nothing. Any fix that only relaxes the write would therefore change nothing --
   IF the second pass saw only new bytes.
3. But it does not. src/cli.rs:1425 calls snapshot_jsonl(.., previous = None, CursorKind::Observation),
   and in src/context/jsonl.rs the no-previous-cursor branch for Observation starts at byte 0. Every
   observe pass re-reads the transcript from the head (capped at OBSERVATION_DELTA_BYTES = 8 MiB) and
   relies on source_event_key dedupe. The stored observation cursor is used for the CAS and written
   forward, but NOT to position the read.
4. So pass 2 does re-pair the tool_use with its result and does compute 'loaded'. The single line that
   throws it away is in record_observations_with_cursor:
       INSERT INTO observations (...) ... ON CONFLICT (source_event_key) DO NOTHING
   The row already exists as 'attempted', so the confirmation is discarded. That is the whole defect.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PLAN. Option (a) in this bead -- retain a bounded pending-association set keyed by
tool_use id -- is unnecessary. There is nothing to retain: the transcript IS the pending state, and it is
already bounded by the existing 8 MiB read cap and the record cap. The fix is a monotone upgrade in the
write, roughly fifteen lines, with no schema change, no new table, no migration, and no new limit.

REFINEMENT 2 IS THEREFORE PARTLY MOOT. It required "a maximum number of pending associations retained per
session" and that "pending state must be counted against something, not kept off the books". Both are
already satisfied by the ingestion cap, because no pending state is retained. What survives from it is the
age bound: a result that arrives after the invocation has fallen outside the capped read window is never
re-paired and the row stays 'attempted' -- an undercount, which is the conservative direction.

REFINEMENT 2 also required that expiry be RECORDED rather than silent, so a reader can tell "never
confirmed" from "confirmation arrived too late". I am NOT implementing that, and the reason is concrete:
observations.evidence_state carries CHECK(evidence_state IN ('attempted','loaded','censored')), so a
terminal-expired state needs a migration, and there is no spare column. Recording it per row is a schema
change I do not think this defect justifies. Deferred explicitly rather than quietly dropped.

REFINEMENT 1 STANDS AND IS CHEAP HERE. Upgrading only evidence_state means attributed_event_id is not
touched, so attribution cannot be recomputed by construction. I am also NOT moving observed_at_unix_ms,
which refinement 1 asked for, and this one I think the refinement got wrong: attribution was computed FROM
that timestamp by the 30-minute lookback, so moving the timestamp forward while freezing the attribution
makes the row internally inconsistent -- a reader recomputing attribution would get a different event. The
load happened when it was first observed. The confirmation time is not retained, and saying so is better
than storing a time that means neither thing.

MONOTONE RULE I WILL IMPLEMENT. attempted -> loaded only, when the incoming evidence is loaded. Never
loaded -> attempted. A failed result, or a success carrying error lines, stays attempted, mirroring
src/context/tool.rs:446 exactly. 'censored' is left alone: it is a distinct state per AGENTS.md, not a
weaker form of attempted.

SEPARATE FINDING, NOT THIS BEAD, worth its own issue: because the observe read starts at byte 0 and caps
at 8 MiB, a transcript larger than 8 MiB is observed only from its HEAD, and unread_backlog is set. If the
CLI does not loop on that backlog, observation for a long session would never reach recent events. I have
not verified the CLI's handling yet and am not scope-creeping into it here; filing once I have evidence
either way rather than speculating in a bead.

title: Two roster_resolution cases pass on RCH workers and fail on this host: a symlink escape records no diagnostic
design:
## What fails

At main (77f302b), on threadripperje, deterministically and in 0.01s:

- `roster_resolution::authorized_file_symlink_deduplicates_but_escape_withholds_authority`
  (tests/roster_resolution.rs:651) — expects a `ResolutionError::Read` diagnostic for
  a `SKILL.md` symlinked to a file outside the authorized root;
- `roster_resolution::malformed_winner_withholds_its_name_but_unsupported_layout_claims_no_name`
  (tests/roster_resolution.rs:497) — expects a diagnostic for an unsupported nested
  layout.

Instrumented, the first one's diagnostics vector is **empty**: `PROBE escape
diagnostics: []`. The exclusion itself is correct — `is_partial()` holds and
`exact_name("escape")` is `Missing` — but nothing records *why*, so a `--why-not` or
roster-evidence consumer sees an excluded entry with no reason.

## Why nobody noticed

The same 15 cases pass on the fleet: `full6.log` and `full7.log` both report
`roster_resolution ... 15 passed; 0 failed` on vmi1227854, while this host reports
13 passed / 2 failed. Every shared gate runs on the fleet, so the green suite is not
evidence for a developer's own machine — nor, more importantly, for a user's.

## What I ruled out

- **Not my change.** Reverting `src/pipeline.rs` and `src/storage/ledger.rs` to main
  and rebuilding reproduces both failures (13 passed / 2 failed), so they predate
  today's provider-attempt work.
- **Not load.** They fail with `--test-threads=1` in an otherwise idle target, in
  0.41s. By contrast the other nine failures in the same local full-suite run are
  load artifacts: `rank_acceptance` passes 56/0 and `subprocess_contract` passes 14/0
  when run serially.
- **Not the effective uid.** They fail as uid 1000 and as root on this host, which is
  the opposite of sr-61j8.
- **Not the temp filesystem alone.** They fail with the fixture on tmpfs (`/tmp`) and
  with `TMPDIR` pointed at btrfs (`/data/...`).

So the discriminator is something else about the host or its kernel, and the
mechanism — why the escaping candidate never reaches `roots.read_absolute` here, and
does on a worker — is undetermined. That is the first thing to find.

## Why it matters

Either the product records no reason for a symlink-escape exclusion on some hosts,
which is a silent exclusion of exactly the kind this project keeps fixing, or the
test asserts something host-specific. Both need an answer before the roster evidence
surface can be trusted, and both are invisible to a fleet-only gate.
notes:
Two-sided measurement, same instrumented test, same revision:

- worker vmi1227854 (via `rch exec`): `PROBE bad: partial=true advisory=1
  diagnostics=["1:Read"] skills=[2]`, escape resolution `Missing` — test passes.
- this host: `PROBE bad: partial=true advisory=1 diagnostics=[] skills=[2]`, escape
  resolution `Missing` — test fails only on the diagnostic assertion.

Everything else is identical, including the dedup result (one skill, two bindings) and
the advisory count. Candidate index 1 is the escape, since the three directories sort
`alias`, `escape`, `original`. So the worker records `EscapesAuthorizedRoots` mapped
to `Read` and this host records nothing for the same fixture.

Leads for whoever picks this up, and one dead end I already walked:

- **Not the `d_type` branch.** `src/roster/discovery.rs:472` handles both a reported
  `Type::Symlink` and a `None` `d_type` (via `fstatat` with `AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW`),
  and both paths call `push_candidate` for a name matching the skill file. So the
  escape should become a candidate on any filesystem.
- Therefore the divergence is downstream of discovery: either `read_absolute` does
  not refuse the target here, or the candidate is dropped before it. Worth printing
  the candidate list and each candidate's read outcome in
  `src/roster/resolution.rs` around the `roots.read_absolute` call.
- The escape file's content is `# Outside\n\nprivate`, with no frontmatter. If the
  read succeeds here, the missing-frontmatter fallback path becomes the suspect, and
  the entry could be dropped as an excluded record without a diagnostic — which
  would make the silent branch a real defect rather than a test artifact.

Confirmed fixed from the reporting side (MagentaSquirrel, 2026-09-20). This bead was
filed because two roster_resolution cases passed on RCH worker vmi1227854 and failed on
threadripperje, which is the host I run on. A full suite at c1440f4 plus my unrelated
stats changes, run on threadripperje, is 126 reports / 1160 passed / 0 failed / 10
ignored -- the two cases now pass on the host where they used to fail, so the
host-dependence is gone rather than merely unobserved.

title: jev_transport shutdown is bounded by an already-expired remainder, so draining gets ~1ms under load
design:
## What happens

`tests/jev_transport.rs`'s `Harness::finish` asserts `invocation.shutdown()`, and
`ProcessInvocation::shutdown` bounds the drain by `remaining_until_expiry()`, with
`max(remaining, 1)` as the floor. The deadline cases in that file deliberately run
until the invocation's budget is gone, so by the time `finish` runs, the bound is
one millisecond and draining owned threads fails.

## Measured

Inside a full-suite run on vmi1227854 at b9e8b34's tree,
`handshake_and_body_deadlines_close_owned_connections` failed at
`tests/jev_transport.rs:90` with "owned runtime must shut down". The case's own
recorded document in the same output shows the behaviour under test was correct:
`{"case_id":"slow-handshake","connection_closed":true,"decision":"refused",
"elapsed_ms":1541,"failure_kind":"Deadline"}`. Re-run alone at the same tree it
passes (1 passed, 1.88s), so the transport boundary is fine and the assertion after
it is what breaks.

## Family

This is sr-5n0b one test over: there, the entry budget was spent by the runtime
construction it was measured against; here it is spent by the work, leaving the
shutdown no room. `tests/roster_resolution.rs` already anticipated the shape in a
comment — "otherwise shutdown has only 1 ms to drain threads" — and works around it
by keeping the harness invocation separate from the deliberately expired clock.

## Suggested fix

Either give `finish` its own drain bound rather than inheriting the expired
invocation's remainder, or follow roster_resolution and keep the harness invocation
distinct from the clock the case expires. What it must not do is drop the assertion:
"the owned runtime shuts down" is a real property, and the deadline cases are
exactly where a leaked thread would hide.
close_reason: Fixed in 3dd7f84: Run::new now builds two clocks, the short one for the client (unchanged deadline behaviour) and a generous one owning the runtime, so shutdown is not bounded by a deadline the case deliberately expired. Same remedy tests/roster_resolution.rs already used. Assertions untouched: the deadline case still requires TransportErrorKind::Deadline, a started HTTP attempt, a server-side close and completion inside three seconds. fmt and clippy clean; target passes three consecutive runs. Not established: the original failure was never reproduced locally (CPU saturation does not trigger it, per the sr-5n0b measurements), so this removes the coupling rather than demonstrating before/after.
