title: Count hook failures that occur before the first ledger write in the availability denominator
description:
## Problem

The availability gate (.8.4: ≤5% operational fallback over ≥500 representative
hook invocations) is computed from ledger rows, but **hook failures that occur
before the first ledger write leave no row at all**. The context/overlay stage
returns early (`src/pipeline.rs:1083-1115`) and the earliest recording is
`record_inflight_ranking` (`pipeline.rs:2330`). By the hook contract those
failures are exit 0 + empty stdout + a stderr line nobody keeps, so they are
invisible everywhere. The denominator is therefore biased toward success: a
build that fails context capture on most sessions can still report a low
fallback rate over the sessions it managed to record.

## Evidence (2026-09-22)

- The 05:28–05:43Z wave: 6 real user prompts across 4 sessions with the hook
  installed and **zero ledger rows** (pre-fix sr-t034 binary).
- After the fix: session e2edf818 at 17:28:06Z and a83ca4ec at 17:28:12Z left
  no rows; e2edf818 reproduces as `Transcript branch cannot be resolved`
  (hook_success dead-end bead). The a83ca4ec drop did not reproduce at lower
  load and is unexplained.
- Of 18 real prompts after installation, 11 produced rows (4 of them in
  sessions later shown to fail branch resolution).

## Required behavior

- Every `sr hook claude` invocation that gets far enough to parse the hook
  payload's `session_id`/`cwd` records exactly one outcome for the
  availability cohort, including pre-context failures, with a typed
  reason (`context-malformed`, `ambiguous-branch`, `timeout`, …). Options: a
  minimal `unavailable` ranking_events row keyed by the harness event identity
  (respecting duplicate-delivery rules), or a separate bounded, owner-only
  invocation counter. Must honor `--no-ledger`/`--no-persist` and ledger-absent
  (then report "unmeasured", never zero).
- Invocations that fail before the payload parses are counted in a
  process-local-safe way or explicitly declared as an unmeasurable residual in
  the cohort report.
- `sr stats` reports these separately from provider/credential failures and
  includes them in the operational-fallback denominator.

## Tests

- Each pre-recording failure class (malformed transcript, ambiguous branch,
  missing prompt, session mismatch, overlay deadline) through the real binary in
  an isolated HOME produces one counted outcome, and stats' fallback rate
  includes it.
- Duplicate delivery of the same failing event is counted once.
- `--no-ledger` / absent ledger: nothing written, report says unmeasured.
- Adversarial: a build whose overlay always fails must show ~100% fallback in
  stats, not 0% over zero rows.
close_reason: bd9e4af. The reopened gap is fixed: failure finalization runs on EntryClock::for_failure_finalization (half the cleanup reserve), so a failure at the work deadline records its typed row. Evidence: real-SQLite mechanism test; a replay of the pinned build d103476d over 3 x 40 real transcripts at load 119-140, where every run inside its total deadline recorded exactly one row, in-deadline timeouts included. The remaining residuals (unparseable payloads; runs starved past their own 3,000 ms total, 7/120, 3,141-6,244 ms) are declared in docs/output-contract.md, with sr-01h3 filed to measure them via an entry counter.

comments.author: ubuntu

A replay of HEAD a2dd3a5's hook over 40 real transcripts (offline, no key, isolated ledger, load ~125) gave 35 cache-miss rows and 1 malformed-input row, plus 4 invocations with NO row: 'Transcript overlay deadline exhausted', 'Deadline exceeded during roster validation' x2, 'Runtime cleanup did not finish within the invocation deadline'. Cause: record_failed_attempts writes with the request cx after the work deadline has passed, so the ledger refuses the write. Timeouts are exactly the operational failures the availability denominator needs. Fixing now: record the finished failure inside the cleanup reserve.

title: Record credential-absent separately from provider authentication rejection
description:
## Problem

`src/privacy/mod.rs:269` maps `MissingCredential → ErrorKind::Authentication`,
and the recorded `ranking_events.reason` is `authentication` both when no key is
in the environment and when TypeSafe rejects a key (`pipeline.rs:3713`,
"Invalid credentials"). The shadow deployment pre-registration §7 requires the
cohort report to keep `credential-absent` separate from provider outages and
auth failures. With today's data, 11/11 shadow rows say `authentication` and
nothing in the ledger distinguishes "operator never supplied a key" (an
environment problem, excluded from provider availability) from "the provider
refused the key" (a real outage-class event).

## Required behavior

- A distinct recorded reason/kind for an absent credential (e.g.
  `credential-absent`) versus provider rejection (`authentication`), in the
  ledger and `sr stats` fallback causes. Decide whether the CLI error kind also
  splits (docs/output-contract.md error-kind table and the capabilities exit
  table must stay synchronized; exit code stays 4 unless the contract says
  otherwise). Keep the hook quiet either way.
- Doctor already reports credential `absent`; keep its wording consistent.

## Tests

- No key → recorded reason credential-absent; stats cause breakdown shows it.
- Loopback TLS fixture returning 401 → recorded `authentication`.
- Output-contract/capabilities synchronization test covers the new kind.
close_reason: New ErrorKind credential-absent (exit 4); MissingCredential maps to it, 401/403 stays authentication. sr stats gains turns.failure_causes {reason,count} (table + JSON). Demo unavailable case, output-contract and effect-policies docs updated; hash-pinned fixtures left as valid authentication examples. Tests: ledger_attempt_recording::an_absent_credential_is_recorded_apart_from_a_rejected_key (real binary, loopback TLS 401), stats failure_causes partition, json_envelopes/output_contract/config_contract kind tables.

title: Doctor reports no-advisory-candidates while rank ranks unverified-visibility skills
description:
## Problem

On every real Claude installation `sr doctor` reports roster
`state: "no-advisory-candidates"` (`advisory: 0`, `unverified: 205` on the
maintainer machine) and makes "Run `sr roster --json` to see why each skill is
not offered as advice" its **first** next step. But since 20269ff
("label Claude precedence as provisional and unverified") `sr rank` *does* rank
and suggest unverified-visibility skills, with an `unverified-visibility`
warning (README "Resolve what is loadable"; `src/pipeline.rs:3104`). The real
deployment smoke ranked this very roster. So the readiness report tells a user
their roster is useless while ranking works. `src/readiness.rs:161-175` and
docs/doctor-readiness.md:23-28 still encode the pre-20269ff rule.

## Fix

Doctor's roster readiness must mirror rank's eligibility: count
unverified-but-rankable skills as rankable (a distinct state such as
`ready-unverified`, or `ready` with an `unverified` count and a caveat), and
reserve `no-advisory-candidates` for rosters where rank would genuinely have
nothing eligible (all forbidden/manual-only/ambiguous/shadowed). Update
docs/doctor-readiness.md and the doctor readiness tests.

## Tests

- Real-layout temp roster of Claude personal skills → doctor does not say
  no-advisory-candidates, and `sr rank --dry-run` over the same roster includes
  them (the two agree).
- Roster of only `disable-model-invocation: true` skills → no-advisory-candidates.

title: Two of four exposure states are unreachable: nothing records generated or acknowledged
design:
## What I found

`ExposureState` has four values and the ledger can write all four, but only two
can occur in production:

- `Prepared`: the only state `src/pipeline.rs:3953` ever writes when recording a
  ranking event.
- `Emitted`: `record_emission`, called from `src/cli.rs`, advances to it.
- `Generated`: no production writer. Nothing outside `src/storage/` constructs it.
- `Acknowledged`: no production caller of `record_acknowledgment` exists at all;
  the only mention outside `src/storage/ledger.rs` is the re-export in
  `src/storage/mod.rs`.

Checked by grepping every `ExposureState` and `record_acknowledgment` reference in
`src/` outside the storage module at c62d526; the writer and its transitions are
tested (`tests/ledger_exposure_lifecycle_contract.rs`), which is why this is
invisible from the test suite.

## Why it is worth a bead rather than a shrug

Nothing misreports today, because no command surfaces exposure-state counts yet.
The moment one does — P5 statistics are the obvious consumer — a zero
`acknowledged` count reads as "no advisory was ever acknowledged" when the truth
is "we never record acknowledgment". That is the same shape as the defects that
have cost this project the most: a state that is silently never produced, read by
a later consumer as a measured zero.

sr-roadmap-l1i.6.8 ("Record generated, prepared, emitted and acknowledged
separately") is closed with the reason "done". I am not reopening it: the ledger
genuinely can record the four states separately, which is what that bead asked
for. Driving the fourth needs a delivery signal, and Claude's `UserPromptSubmit`
protocol does not give one.

## Options

1. Drive `Acknowledged` from load attribution: an observation that attributes a
   load to an emission is the strongest evidence available that the advisory
   reached the agent. This is 6.9 machinery that already exists.
2. Decide `Acknowledged` is out of scope for v1 and say so where a reader would
   otherwise infer a measured zero — the statistics output and the ledger docs —
   with `unknown` rather than `0`.

Either is fine; leaving both undone is what is not. Whoever takes it should also
decide whether `Generated` is a state this product ever occupies, or dead schema
worth documenting as reserved.
close_reason: Resolved in 226bb73 by documenting it at the type, with the analysis corrected. Prepared and Emitted are the only states with producers; Generated has none because recording follows a decision; Acknowledged has none because nothing available establishes delivery. I had suggested driving Acknowledged from load attribution and withdrew it on reading record_acknowledgment: it requires a verified_delivery_key meaning the harness received the advisory, and an observed load is equally consistent with the agent reaching for that skill unprompted, so using it would convert correlational evidence into a delivery claim. The comment says so where the next implementer will be standing, and names the rendering rule for a future report: not recorded, never a measured zero. Doc-only; fmt and clippy clean.

title: Declare eval --online as a planned flag; capabilities currently overstates the build
description:
## Problem

`sr eval --online` always fails with a generic invalid-usage error ("live batch
execution is not implemented; supply recorded replay cases in offline mode",
`src/evaluation/batch.rs:266`), but `--online` is **absent from
`PLANNED_FLAGS`** (`src/capabilities.rs:45-70`), so `sr capabilities --json`
reports `eval` as implemented with no planned `--online`. Every other
unimplemented command/flag (snooze, budget, calibrate, tui, gaps,
doctor --descriptions, eval --sample-size/--seed/--explain) is refused with its
phase named and listed as planned; this is the only place the capability
contract overstates the build (CLI wiring audit, 2026-09-22).

Add `eval --online` (and `--max-requests`, which only matters with it) to
`PLANNED_FLAGS` with the phase that .6.19 closes, route the refusal through
the planned-flag path (exit 2 naming the phase), and remove the entry when
.6.19 lands live batches. Update the capabilities contract test.

## Tests

- `sr eval --dataset X --online --allow-network --max-requests 1` → planned
  refusal naming the phase; `capabilities --json` lists it under planned flags.

title: Enforce endpoint alpha budgets at small magnitudes
description: Allocator explicit accepts allocations exceeding tiny total_alpha by orders of magnitude because it adds absolute1e-9 slack. equal_split silently merges duplicate names and can return zero alpha after underflow. Reject invalid endpoint sets and overspending, keep total budget immutable after construction, validate divided allocations, preserve ordinary valid split/explicit cases. Add adversarial old-source failures and fixed verification; no statistical-coverage proof claimed by numeric budgeting alone.
close_reason: Independent review (FuchsiaCave; the requested RubyCat review never happened) at origin/main 270797e: 3edff71 and 80958a1 are on main. Arithmetic checked by hand. alpha_units: a normal binary64 is m*2^(e-1075) = m*2^(e-1) units of 2^-1074, so shift=e-1; a subnormal is its fraction, shift 0. For alpha<1, e<=1022 gives word<=15, so 15-word never underflows, and the low-word << truncation is recovered by >>(64-offset). Accumulation carries from word 16 to 0, the array comparison is big-endian lexicographic, and partial sums stay below 2^1075 units, within 17x64 bits. equal_split rejects empty, blank and duplicate names; a zero share from underflow is caught by validate_alpha; round-up is repaired by next_down and revalidation, with no slack. total_alpha is private with a getter only. Tests: evaluation_alpha_budget's six cases (sub-ULP excess in both orders at 0.5, 1e-12, 1e-100 and 1e-300, each with a success twin; every power of two in (0,1) including subnormals, exact-boundary ok and one-ULP-over err) passed in all three of my full local suite runs today. title: Scope roster authority withholding to affected invocation names
description:
Found during P2 acceptance review (sr-roadmap-l1i.3.17, CopperWren). Observed with a real tree in tests/p2_gate.rs.

Current behavior (src/roster/resolution.rs, resolve_claude_plan, from e0bc2b2 / 3.5):
1. Any per-record diagnostic sets `incomplete`, and every entry is downgraded to Visibility::Unverified. This covers malformed metadata, an unsupported layout, a read failure, a changed file and the limit. So one malformed SKILL.md anywhere in the project or personal roots leaves zero advisory candidates for the whole roster. The test malformed_winner_and_unsupported_layout_withhold_authority asserts exactly this, including an unrelated nested layout disabling a differently named skill.
2. A read failure (for example a SKILL.md symlink escaping the root, or an unreadable file) does `break`. Every later candidate is then dropped even from inspection, so sr roster and sr doctor under-report skills after the first unreadable file.

Why it matters: real personal skill directories commonly contain one broken file. The README promises that "Ambiguous skill metadata excludes that record and marks coverage partial" and that "A partial roster can support a scoped positive recommendation when the target and its restrictions are verified". Neither holds while one bad file anywhere removes all advisory authority. It is fail-closed, so not a safety defect, but it makes advice unavailable.

Proposed scope (to be decided by the owner, not assumed):
(a) Withhold authority only for the invocation names the failed record could claim. The name is known from the directory layout for SKILL.md files. When the name is unknowable, such as an unsupported layout, keep the global withholding.
(b) Continue past a per-file read error, recording it, so later records stay inspectable.
(c) Keep root-level failures (unreadable root, walk limits) global.
Acceptance: one malformed or escaping file among valid ones leaves the other names advisory and inspectable, while a same-name malformed winner still withholds that name. Update malformed_winner_and_unsupported_layout_withhold_authority deliberately, keeping its same-name assertion, and extend tests/p2_gate.rs.

title: prune --apply advances the data generation even when it prunes nothing
close_reason: Withdrawn by the filer as not-a-defect. The data generation is a store-wide optimistic-concurrency version advanced by nine functions including ordinary observation, emission and feedback recording, not a destroyed-history marker, so prune's unconditional bump is consistent with the design and the severity argument's premise was false. Correction comment records what I got wrong and why.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
`sr ledger prune --apply` advances the store's data generation unconditionally, including when it
deletes nothing at all.

OBSERVED, driving the real binary at main 333d04b in an isolated owner-only HOME with one recorded
observation and a default 30-day cutoff, so nothing was old enough to prune:

    $ sr ledger prune --apply --json
    "events_pruned": 0, "candidates_pruned": 0, "observations_pruned": 0,
    "judgments_pruned": 0, "provider_attempts_pruned": 0, "snapshots_pruned": 0,
    "stamp_before": { "schema_generation": 2, "data_generation": 2 },
    "stamp_after":  { "schema_generation": 2, "data_generation": 3 },
    "affected_provenance": "ordinary-retention-prune"

MECHANISM: `src/storage/ledger.rs`, in `prune_apply`, immediately after the DELETE statements:

    let new_data_gen = expected_stamp.data_generation.checked_add(1)...
    tx.execute("UPDATE store_meta SET data_generation = ?1 WHERE singleton = 1", ...)

There is no condition on any delete having affected a row. The bump is part of the same transaction
whether the prune removed two thousand events or none.

WHY THIS LOOKS WRONG RATHER THAN MERELY ODD. AGENTS.md ties the generation's purpose to a specific
hazard: "clear advances the data generation so a ranking/observer started before it cannot repopulate
cleared history from stale in-memory work", and "Optional old-generation recording is skipped with a
diagnostic; required feedback/admin writes fail rather than resurrect removed evidence." The hazard is
resurrection of removed evidence. A prune that removed nothing has removed no evidence, so there is
nothing for a stale writer to resurrect, yet every writer holding the previous generation is now
invalidated by `src/storage/ledger.rs:2286`'s `actual.data_generation != expected.data_generation`
check.

Consequences, in the documented severity order:
- An in-flight ranking's optional ledger recording is skipped with a diagnostic. Evidence lost.
- An in-flight `sr feedback` is a required write, so it fails rather than degrading -- exit 9
  storage-failure on a user-facing command, because an unrelated no-op prune ran beside it.

Retention cleanup is documented to run outside hooks, so this needs concurrency to bite. But a
periodic prune on a quiet machine is exactly the case where nothing is ever old enough to remove, and
it would bump the generation on every run, each time breaking whatever happened to be writing.

HONESTY ABOUT WHAT I DID AND DID NOT SHOW. I demonstrated the unconditional bump against the real
binary, as quoted above. I did NOT demonstrate a concurrent writer losing its row or a `sr feedback`
failing because of it: each CLI invocation re-reads the stamp, so producing the race by hand is not
possible, and it belongs in an in-process test. The consequence above is reasoned from the generation
check and the documented contract, not observed. Treat the bump as fact and the consequence as
argument.

EXISTING COVERAGE: `tests/ledger_retention_contract.rs:327` asserts
`report.stamp_after.data_generation == stamp.data_generation + 1`, but only in a case where
`events_pruned == 2`. The zero-row case is unpinned in either direction, which is why this could drift
in without anyone noticing.

SUGGESTED FIX AND TEST:
- Advance the data generation only when the prune actually removed something. The `PruneReport`
  already carries every count needed for that decision, and `affected_provenance:
  "ordinary-retention-prune"` suggests the design already means to distinguish an ordinary retention
  pass from a `clear`.
- Two tests, since this is the kind of invariant that wants both directions: a prune that removes rows
  must advance the generation (already covered at :327), and a prune that removes nothing must leave
  it untouched.
- If the unconditional bump turns out to be deliberate -- for instance if a partially-applied delete
  could leave a writer referencing a row that is gone -- then say so in a comment at that line and pin
  it with a test asserting the no-op bump, because right now the code reads as an oversight and
  nothing records the intent either way.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CORRECTION BY THE FILER, about twenty minutes after filing. This bead is wrong and I am withdrawing
it. The observation it rests on is real; the conclusion I drew from it is not.

What I filed: that `prune_apply` advancing the data generation on a zero-row prune is a defect, because
the generation exists to stop a stale writer resurrecting removed evidence, and a prune that removed
nothing created no such hazard. I reasoned -- and labelled as reasoned, not observed -- that an
in-flight `sr feedback` would therefore fail with exit 9 because an unrelated no-op prune ran beside it.

What I then found, continuing to drive the same sandbox. An `sr observe` that recorded ZERO
observations also advanced the generation, 5 -> 6, while a plain `sr ledger status` did not. That did
not fit my model, so I enumerated every site that advances it:

    prune_apply, clear_apply, revise_judgment, remove_judgment, record_observations_with_cursor,
    record_paired_correction, record_single_feedback, record_emission, record_acknowledgment

Nine functions, and the last five are ordinary, entirely non-destructive recording. So the data
generation is not a "history was destroyed" marker at all. It is a store-wide optimistic-concurrency
version bumped by every mutation, which is exactly what AGENTS.md describes when it says "Every
mutation checks the expected store incarnation and schema/data generation inside its transaction".

That makes `prune_apply`'s unconditional bump consistent with the rest of the store rather than an
oversight, and it makes my stated consequence not specific to prune at all: any concurrent mutation
moves the version, so a writer that cannot tolerate the version moving under it would be broken in
ordinary use, not just beside a prune. The premise of my severity argument was false.

The residue, for completeness and not as a defect: a zero-row prune performs one UPDATE to bump a
version when no data changed, and the `observe` case I measured was not truly a no-op either -- it
re-committed the cursor (`cursor_generation` 1 -> 2), so its bump was a genuine write. Nothing here is
worth changing.

What I should have done before filing: enumerate the writers of a field before theorising about what
its movement means. I had the grep output that would have told me -- the earlier `data_generation`
search in this same investigation listed line 4727 in `record_observations_with_cursor` -- and I read
past it because I had already formed a model from the prune site and the AGENTS.md sentence about
`clear`. Closing as not-a-defect. The evidence quoted in the original comment stays accurate as a
record of behaviour; only my interpretation of it was wrong.

title: Dogfood polish: oversized SKILL.md unreadable, persistence never reports healthy, relative --transcript rejected
description:
Three smaller things found by installing the release binary of 221494f and using it on a real machine. Each is independent of sr-xlf6 and sr-un4j.

1. A legitimately large SKILL.md is reported as unreadable. ~/.claude/skills/hfdt/SKILL.md is 508 KB and lands in record_causes as {unreadable: 1}. Real skills do get this big (the next largest here are 174 KB and 139 KB, which are accepted). Whatever bound rejects it should either be raised or, at minimum, the cause should say oversized rather than unreadable, since unreadable suggests a permissions or IO fault. Via sr-xlf6 this single file also currently poisons the entire roster.

2. The persistence field can never report a healthy store. Evaluated::persistence() in src/pipeline.rs returns only "disabled" (when the ledger is disabled) or "unavailable" - there is no third arm. Every ordinary ranked document therefore says persistence: unavailable even when nothing is wrong, which cost me real time while diagnosing sr-un4j because it looks like a storage fault. Either report the actual state or, while the ledger is unimplemented, name the field for what it measures.

3. A relative --transcript path is rejected with a misleading error. `sr rank --transcript ../session.jsonl --harness claude_code` fails with exit 7 malformed-input "Transcript snapshot failed: transcript path is not a regular file". The same file via an absolute path works. Either resolve the path against the invocation's cwd (the workspace join already happens for the session-identity lookup at src/pipeline.rs:637-641) or say that the path must be absolute. The current message asserts something untrue about the file.

Context worth keeping: apart from these and the two bugs above, the product performed well in real use. Ranking 204 real skills against a real 44 MB session transcript took 1.8 s end to end including both Jev calls, history was correctly windowed, and the suggestions were apt (agent-mail at fits 0.94 for a multi-agent file-clobbering request; rust-tester at 0.91 for failing cargo tests; reality-check-for-project at 0.73 for the actual live task). No credential ever appeared in output.
close_reason:
Independent review approved by MistyCoyote:
- Verified ResolutionError::Oversized distinguishes oversized skills from unreadable permissions/IO errors (tested in tests/roster_real_layout.rs: an_oversized_skill_is_reported_as_oversized_not_unreadable).
- Verified Evaluated::persistence() truthful reporting of disabled / recorded / unavailable states (tested in tests/cache_live_reuse.rs).
- Verified relative --transcript resolution against workspace (tested in tests/cache_live_reuse.rs).
- All tests pass remotely via RCH.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CopperWren: all three items now resolved across two commits.

C1 oversized SKILL.md (0e64f5c). resolve_claude_plan discarded the ReadError and recorded ResolutionError::Read for every failure, so a 508 KB SKILL.md over the 256 KiB SKILL_FILE_BYTES bound was reported as record cause 'unreadable'. It is present, permitted and readable, just too large to parse, and that label sent me looking for a permissions fault while dogfooding. ReadError::TooLarge now maps to a new ResolutionError::Oversized, reported as 'oversized'. Exclusion and per-name withholding are unchanged, since an oversized file could legitimately claim that name, and Oversized deliberately joins Read in the snapshot-incompleteness rule because the entry's content is still unknown - leaving it out would have quietly widened what counts as a complete snapshot. One assertion in SilentFinch's tests/roster_resolution.rs follows the sharper cause: that test writes SKILL_FILE_BYTES.max()+1 and asserted Read, so it now asserts Oversized, which is what its own fixture describes; its other assertions are untouched and still pass.

C2 persistence never reporting healthy (b8d44c8). Evaluated::persistence() had no arm that could return 'recorded' even though the output contract already allowed it, so it answered 'unavailable' in runs where cache.hit, wide_hit and rerank_hit were all true. It now reports disabled / recorded / unavailable truthfully, and docs/output-contract.md pins the three states.

C3 relative --transcript path (b8d44c8). The session attribution resolved a relative path against the workspace while the read used it raw, so a perfectly good transcript was refused as 'not a regular file'. Both now resolve once.

Evidence: new tests/roster_real_layout.rs (2 cases) and tests/cache_live_reuse.rs (4 cases), all with the real binary and all offline. Planted negatives: the roster pair fails on the unfixed source reporting the misleading 'unreadable' cause, and all four cache cases fail on the unfixed source. Full suite at 0e64f5c's tree: 895 passed, 0 failed, 10 ignored across 97 reports, required-remote on vmi1227854 (76.5s). rustfmt clean on every owned file.

Mine is 508 KB and two others here are 174 KB and 139 KB, so the bound is plausible but the largest real skill in my library is excluded from ranking entirely. Ranking only needs the frontmatter description, which has its own 16 KiB bound, so reading a bounded head rather than refusing the file would keep such skills rankable. title: Deliver TYPESAFE_API_KEY to hook processes: 11/11 shadow turns are credential-absent, zero cohort evaluations
description:
## Problem

The self-hosted shadow deployment (sr-1uf4, receipt 2026-09-22 06:24Z) has
produced **zero successful hook evaluations**. Live ledger at 17:58Z, ~11.5 h
after deployment: shadow channel 11 turns, **11 `unavailable / authentication`**,
0 abstain, 0 ranked. All 3 provider attempts ever recorded (21,738 tokens) are
the manual deployment smoke, not hook traffic.

Root cause: agent processes are not launched with `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, so hook
children inherit none. `src/privacy/mod.rs:269` maps
`MissingCredential → ErrorKind::Authentication`. Verified in the reviewer's own
Claude session: the key is absent from the agent shell (hooks get the same
environment). The deployment comment already said "until the key is present
when the agent process starts, every shadow turn records unavailable", and it
was treated as operator discipline; nothing changed in 11 hours and no bead
owned it.

## Constraints

- AGENTS.md/README: credentials are environment-only; never serialized into
  config; never printed, logged or committed. Do not add a credential file
  reader to `sr` as a workaround.
- Blocked on the consent-scope decision (companion bead): do not deliver the
  key to hook processes until the scope matches the pre-registration.

## Options (maintainer choice)

1. Export the key in the environment that launches agent sessions (e.g. the
   ntm/cc launcher or a login-shell snippet that reads the Vault copy with
   tracing off), so every agent process has it. Broadest; covers all projects.
2. A trusted wrapper for the hook command that loads the key from Vault/`.env`
   and `exec`s `sr hook claude`. Requires the installer to support a wrapper
   path or a documented manual edit; must keep the absolute trusted path and
   timeout semantics (and the wrapper's own startup counts against the 4 s
   outer timeout).

## Acceptance

- After the change, a fresh Claude session's first prompt produces a shadow row
  whose decision is not `authentication` (ranked/abstain, or an honest provider
  failure), verified with `sr stats --json` against the real ledger.
- 24 h later: the shadow channel's credential-absent share is reported and near
  zero for in-scope workspaces.
- Receipt appended to docs/self-host-shadow-deployment.md.

title: Hook drops every session with a PreToolUse hook_success attachment: dead-end records make the branch ambiguous
description:
## Problem (found by the 2026-09-22 evening reality check, reproduced at HEAD 09f93b8)

`sr hook claude` silently fails on ordinary long Claude Code sessions with
`sr: Transcript branch cannot be resolved` (exit 0, empty stdout, **no ledger
row**). The trigger is not exotic: Claude Code writes an `attachment` record of
type `hook_success` every time a `PreToolUse` hook produces output, and that
record is a **dead-end child** of a node whose main chain continues. On this
fleet the RCH `PreToolUse:Bash` hook (`/home/ubuntu/.local/bin/rch`) does this
on every intercepted cargo command, so a session becomes un-rankable after its
first intercepted build and stays that way while the dead end is in the
bounded tail.

## Evidence

- This reviewer's own session transcript (2f967675…): 421 main-chain nodes,
  **5 leaves** = 1 real leaf (latest assistant `tool_use`) + 4
  `attachment/hook_success` dead ends, all `hookName: PreToolUse:Bash`,
  `command: /home/ubuntu/.local/bin/rch`. The real hook recorded this session
  at 17:57:55Z (1 prompt, no dead ends yet); ~40 minutes of normal work later,
  both the deployed binary (5dcdb9a) and a HEAD build fail it.
- Session e2edf818…: its bounded tail has 683 nodes and the same 4
  hook_success dead ends + 1 real leaf; same failure on deployed and HEAD.
- Session 3f99ab81… (no dead ends in its tail window) passes context capture.
- `grep hook_success` over src/, tests/ and every bead: zero hits. No fixture
  models this record shape.

## Mechanism

`src/context/overlay.rs:410-425`: when the submitted prompt is not yet in the
transcript (the normal `UserPromptSubmit` case), the overlay calls
`resolve_active_branch` with no target and needs a unique leaf; ambiguity maps
to `OverlayError::AmbiguousBranch` (`overlay.rs:420`, then
`pipeline.rs:1107-1110`). Commit 00c75b3 correctly keeps unmodeled harness
records as lineage **pass-through** nodes so a mid-chain attachment does not
shatter lineage — but a pass-through node with no children then competes as a
leaf (`AmbiguousSiblingForks`, `src/context/branch.rs:110`).

## Required behavior

1. For leaf selection, a node that carries no conversation event (unmodeled /
   pass-through harness records: attachments including `hook_success`,
   `hook_non_blocking_error`, `total_tokens_reminder`, queue/mode markers, …)
   is **not a candidate leaf**. Prune such dead ends iteratively (a chain of
   pass-through dead ends collapses entirely) before counting leaves.
2. Genuine conversation forks — two message-bearing leaves (e.g. a rewind or an
   edited prompt) — **stay ambiguous** exactly as today. Do not introduce
   physical-file-order tie-breaking; that invariant is deliberate.
3. Pass-through nodes that lie *on* the path from root to the real leaf remain
   lineage links, unchanged.
4. Diagnostics stay sanitized; no transcript text in errors.

## Tests (all required)

- Fixture from the real shape: main chain with 4 `hook_success` dead ends off
  mid-chain assistant/tool nodes → resolves to the real leaf; overlay succeeds.
- Chain of two pass-through dead ends (attachment → attachment, no message) →
  still pruned.
- **Boundary pair** (both sides): pass-through dead end + a genuine
  message-bearing sibling fork → still `AmbiguousBranch`; and the same fork with
  no dead ends → still ambiguous (proves pruning did not mask forks).
- Pass-through node mid-path is still traversed (regression for 00c75b3).
- End-to-end: `sr hook claude` over a synthetic transcript with the dead-end
  shape, isolated HOME/XDG, no network → reaches the network-consent stage
  (i.e. context capture succeeded), exit 0, zero stdout.
- Replay the real-transcript probe (scratch script used in the review:
  isolated XDG_CONFIG/DATA/CACHE, no credential, real HOME for roster) on at
  least three live session transcripts containing hook_success records and
  record the result in this bead.

## Why it matters

This is the dominant reason the self-hosted shadow cohort (sr-1uf4) cannot
accumulate: even after the credential problem is fixed, most Rust agent
sessions on this fleet would drop out silently, and because the failure happens
before any ledger write, the availability gate (.8.4) would not even see them
(see the companion bead on counting pre-recording failures). After the fix,
the installed hook binary must be rebuilt from main and redeployed (sr-1uf4
receipt must record the new SHA256 and revision).
close_reason: Implemented and verified (self-verified): tests with planted negative, 12 test binaries green, real-transcript replay 6/10 -> 9/10

Pruning covers system dead ends (placeholders incl. hook_success/hook_non_blocking_error, parentless informational notices) and tool results filed under their own call while the call continues (parallel calls). Evidence, re-executed by me (SELF-verified, not independent): new branch_identity/context_overlay_safety tests fail on the pre-change resolver and pass after; 6 context binaries + 6 hook/observation/pipeline binaries green (remote via RCH); release-build replay of sr hook claude over all 10 recent real transcripts (isolated sandbox, no key/network/ledger): deployed 5dcdb9a 6/10 past context capture, this change 9/10. comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
`rank_acceptance::persistence_reports_disabled_only_when_the_user_disabled_it` fails intermittently on
main, and it is a SEMANTIC failure rather than a timing one, which is why it is worth a bead instead of
a shrug.

OBSERVED at main 0d6744a, `cargo test --locked --no-fail-fast -j 4`, nightly-2026-08-31,
tests/rank_acceptance.rs:1648:

    assertion `left == right` failed
      left: String("recorded")
     right: "unavailable"

DENOMINATOR, stated because "flaky" is a claim and not an observation: it passed in three whole-suite
runs (one at a6f1ff0, two at 0d6744a) and failed in one (0d6744a, pristine main with no local changes).
One failure in four runs on a host whose load average ranged from 30 to 338 today.

THE DOCUMENT IT PRODUCED, key fields, captured from the assertion message:

    "decision": "abstain", "reason": "low-need", "persistence": "recorded", "elapsed_ms": 1802,
    "cache": {"hit": false, "wide_hit": false, "rerank_hit": false, "stale": false, "age_ms": null},
    "usage": {"requests": 1, "http_attempts": 1, "input_tokens": 100, "output_tokens": 25,
              "unknown_usage_attempts": 0},
    "roster": {"eligible": 2, "total": 2, "partial": true, "shortlist": 0, "wide_candidates": 2},
    "warnings": ["unverified-visibility" x2, "source-not-enumerated" x2]

WHY I THINK THE TEST IS NOW STALE RATHER THAN THE PRODUCT BEING WRONG, offered as a hypothesis with its
evidence, not a conclusion. The test's own comment reads:

    // By default recording is wanted, but this build has no ledger yet.

That premise no longer holds. The in-flight ranking-event write landed in 727b387 and was extended in
9c3a106, so an invocation can now durably commit a `ranking_events` row before it settles. CopperWren
defined the field's three values in their sr-roadmap-l1i.6.7 comment -- "recorded: this invocation's
ranking_events row was durably committed. Nothing else earns the word. unavailable: persistence was
permitted but nothing was durably recorded" -- and in the same comment wrote that "concrete
follow-through [is] required when the event write lands, so it cannot be forgotten". This looks like
exactly that follow-through arriving as an intermittent red test rather than as a deliberate edit.

If that is right, "recorded" is the truthful answer whenever the row lands, the expectation of
"unavailable" predates the write being wired, and the intermittency is about whether the best-effort
write completes -- note `elapsed_ms: 1802` against a 2,000 ms budget in the failing run, which is the
kind of margin where a best-effort local write either makes it or does not.

WHAT I DID NOT ESTABLISH, so nobody treats the above as settled:
- Why it is intermittent rather than deterministic. I did not instrument the write.
- Not a foreign store, as far as I can see: `sr_command` in that file does `.env_clear()` and sets HOME,
  XDG_CONFIG_HOME and XDG_CACHE_HOME to fixture paths. XDG_DATA_HOME is not set, but with HOME pointed
  inside the fixture the default ledger directory resolves inside it too, so the obvious
  cross-contamination explanation does not hold up. Worth a second pair of eyes.

THE DECISION THIS NEEDS, which is not mine to make: does an abstaining invocation with a usable ledger
legitimately earn `persistence: "recorded"`? If yes, update the expectation AND that stale comment, so
the next reader is not misled the same way. If no -- if an abstain must not commit a row -- the product
changes and the test is already correct. Please do not resolve it by relaxing the assertion without
answering that question first; the field is user-visible and its whole value is that it does not lie.

Filed by RoseCoyote, found while running a control experiment to establish whether an unrelated timing
failure in my own change's gates was mine. It was not; this one turned up in the control.

title: Notification-started turns must be separated from user requests in the relevance cohort (10 of the first 14 live evaluations)
description:
MEASURED by FuchsiaCave, 2026-09-24, from the live ledger after credential delivery started working (d398bb0). Of the first 14 real shadow evaluations in this repository, 10 were for prompts that are Claude <task-notification> envelopes: a background job finished while the agent was idle, so Claude started a NEW turn with a fresh prompt_id. 3 of the 4 'ranked' suggestions were made on them (rch at fit 0.48 and 0.57; commit-and-release at 0.72). sr-jdji (ad28bdd) handles notifications INSIDE a running turn (same prompt_id); this new-turn shape slips past its rule, which deliberately keys on prompt_id.

EVIDENCE: the transcript record whose promptId equals the ledger event_id carries origin.kind='task-notification', promptSource='system', turnOrigin='task_notification', e.g. event f1cd72c7..., record stamped 01:00:19.305Z. But the hook started about 1.2 s BEFORE that record was written (row 01:00:19.570Z, elapsed 1,230 ms), so the overlay cannot see the marker at hook time. AzureJaguar measured that the payload has no origin field.

EFFECT: the shadow cohort's decision mix and any needless-suggestion or harm measure is dominated by harness traffic, not user requests. In advisory mode sr would inject advice into turns the user never started.

OPTIONS: (a) at the hook boundary, treat a prompt that is ENTIRELY Claude's envelope (starts with <task-notification>, contains <task-id>...</task-id>, ends at </task-notification> with nothing else) as a non-turn delivery, recorded like sr-jdji's. A pasted fragment inside a longer user prompt stays a turn. (b) at observe/stats time, reclassify recorded turns whose transcript record has origin.kind task-notification as non-user turns, excluded from cohort denominators. This is authoritative but retroactive, so it cannot stop advisory injection. Recommended: both, with (b) as the cohort's source of truth and (a) as the advisory guard.

TESTS: a real-shape new-turn notification (fresh prompt_id, envelope-only prompt) yields no ranking, no emission and a non-turn record; a user prompt that quotes an envelope inside other text still ranks; observe reclassifies a recorded turn whose record's origin is task-notification, and stats excludes it from decision mixes and harm denominators.
close_reason: RESCOPED and resolved (FuchsiaCave). Not a hook defect: sr-jdji deliberately treats a notification that starts its own turn while the agent is idle as that turn's request, since the agent does act next (tests/context_overlay_safety.rs asserts it). I drafted an envelope-only hook rule and withdrew it, because it would override that decision; the draft is kept in a stash in my clone. The real issue is cohort classification: relevance and needless-suggestion measures judge USER requests. d648bc7 adds frame rule §2.1(4) to docs/relevance-corpus-contract.md: turns are classified by the transcript record's origin.kind (task-notification), which the hook cannot see because Claude writes it after the hook starts, and harness-initiated turns are excluded from relevance and needless denominators. Operational availability still counts them. Whether advisory mode should inject advice into notification-started turns is a separate decision for the advisory gates (.8.6-.8.9).

title: Interleaved parallel-tool batches remain an ambiguous branch for the hook overlay

title: A background-task notification re-invokes the hook with the turn's prompt_id, and sr ranks the notification as the user's request
description:
Measured by AzureJaguar 2026-09-23 in a live Claude Code 2.1.280 session driven through NTM with a probe hook: when a background task finishes mid-turn, Claude runs UserPromptSubmit again. The payload has the same session_id and THE SAME prompt_id as the running turn, no origin field, and prompt = '<task-notification>…'. In the transcript Claude marks it origin.kind=task-notification (sr already classifies that as injected context); the hook payload carries no such marker.
EFFECT IN sr: the overlay treats the hook prompt as authoritative. Its prompt_id matches the turn's user record, so it overwrites that record's text with the notification text and ranks it. The ledger's redelivery rule keeps one row per prompt_id, but a later delivery replaces a failed one: a notification delivery can replace the user's turn row with a ranking of notification text. In advisory mode it could inject advice about notification text into the user's turn. Live evidence: 2 of the first 10 counted hook entries after fabe46a were such deliveries (sr-w4eh).
FIX: at the hook boundary, a payload whose prompt starts with Claude's '<task-notification>' wrapper, and whose prompt_id already names a user record with different text in the transcript, is a harness notification inside a turn, not a user turn. It must not rank, emit, or replace the turn's row. Record it only as a non-turn delivery, so hook_entries can subtract it from 'unrecorded'. A genuine prompt, including one that quotes '<task-notification>' under a new prompt_id, is unaffected.
close_reason: Implemented and verified: notification deliveries inside a running turn are recognized, not ranked or recorded, and counted apart; unit/overlay/e2e green; live NTM probe confirmed; load flakes rerun green

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Fixed (AzureJaguar). CORRECTION to the description: the overlay matches the hook's prompt_id against record UUIDs, and Claude's prompt_id is the separate promptId field every record of a turn carries. So it did not overwrite the user's record; it appended the notification as a fresh current request and ranked it. Same effect.
Fix: while reading the tail, the overlay notes whether a type=user record carries this promptId and is not itself a task notification (the turn's own prompt or a tool result): proof that a real turn began under this id. If the hook prompt starts with '<task-notification>' and such a record exists, it returns OverlayError::NotificationInTurn. The pipeline then disarms the pre-context failure row, counts the invocation in a second counter (hook-non-turns.log, same rules as sr-01h3's), and exits quietly without ranking. sr stats hook_entries gains non_turn_deliveries, and unrecorded = counted - recorded - non_turn_deliveries. prune/clear apply to both counters. Genuine prompts are unaffected: the wrapper text under a new prompt id, a redelivery of the turn's own text, and a notification that started its own turn while idle all still rank. Also corrected dab9100's 'harness cancellations' wording (from sr-w4eh's disproven premise) in docs/output-contract.md, the HookEntryReport docs and the stats table.

title: Derive CLI failure exit codes from the typed error kind instead of hand-writing them
close_reason: 25383ef. All three items left open in the 02:45 comment are done. (1) missing-snapshot was already remapped by ad51d2c (sr-41a6). (2) revision-conflict is now a documented storage kind (exit 9, was published as cache-miss/11). (3) Mechanism: failure() takes ErrorKind and derives the code; every pipeline.rs and submodule site was converted by per-kind ast-grep rewrites after a script confirmed each code equalled its documented exit. contract-violation -> output-limit; ambiguous-branch is a documented session kind (exit 3). comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
`src/pipeline.rs` builds CLI failures through a stringly-typed helper whose exit code is hand-written
at each call site:

    fn failure(code: u8, kind: &'static str, message: impl Into<String>) -> PipelineFailure
    pub type PipelineFailure = (u8, &'static str, String);

Nothing ties that `code` to that `kind`. The documented mapping lives in the `error_kinds!` macro in
`src/output/mod.rs`, which derives each kind's exit from `CliExit` and is drift-proof; the 71 call
sites in pipeline.rs bypass it entirely. `src/cli.rs:852` returns the hand-written `code` as the
process exit, while the JSON envelope's `error.code` comes from `kind.exit_code()`
(`OutputDocument::failure_with_details`) -- so the two can disagree across the boundary.

I scanned all 71 pairs against the documented table. Ten disagree with it:

1. `src/pipeline.rs:889` -- `failure(2, "ambiguous-session", ...)`. Documented exit for
   `ambiguous-session` is 3 (session), not 2 (usage/config). Note lines 879-883, six lines above,
   do it correctly: `err.kind().exit_code() as u8, err.kind().as_str()`.

2. Eight sites use the kind string `"contract-violation"` with code 5
   (lines 632, 1421, 1681, 1793, 2559, 2816, 3005, 4784). That string is not in the documented
   stable-kind set at all.

3. `src/pipeline.rs:1104` uses `"ambiguous-branch"` with code 7; also not a documented kind.

What happens to an undocumented kind: `src/cli.rs:862-877` looks the string up in `ErrorKind::ALL`,
and on a miss falls back to a code-keyed guess. So `contract-violation` would be published as
`empty-roster` and `ambiguous-branch` as `malformed-input` -- semantically different documented kinds.
A consumer branching on the stable kind would read "your roster is empty" for an internal
output-envelope failure.

REACHABILITY, which is why this is priority 3 and not priority 1. I checked each before filing, and
none of the ten is reachable by a user today:

- The `ambiguous-session` site is the `SelectionOutcome::NeedsChoice` arm, and
  `src/context/source.rs:449` returns `Err(SourceError::AmbiguousSession)` before constructing
  `NeedsChoice` whenever `interactive == false`. `rank` hard-codes `false` (pipeline.rs:858). I
  verified the live path behaves correctly: two sessions in one workspace, no `--latest`, gives
  process exit 3 with `{"code":3,"kind":"ambiguous-session"}` -- code and kind agreeing, through the
  typed site, not this one.
- The eight `contract-violation` sites are `map_err` arms on our own `with_trace`/`from_value`
  re-validation, so they fire only when a trace sr itself built violates `validate_trace`
  (`src/output/mod.rs:988`) -- an internal defect, not user input.
- `ambiguous-branch` is on the Claude hook overlay path, and `src/cli.rs:853` gives hook invocations
  sanitized stderr and exit 0, so the kind is never published there.

So this is latent correctness, not a live mislabel. It becomes live the moment anyone wires
interactive session selection (the TUI/P9 work would) or publishes an overlay error outside the hook
boundary, and it is silent until then.

SUGGESTED FIX, mechanism first so the class cannot come back:
- Change `failure()` to take `ErrorKind` and derive the code (`kind.exit_code() as u8`), making a
  wrong pair unrepresentable. 71 call sites, mechanical, but pipeline.rs is a hot file -- worth
  coordinating so it does not collide with in-flight work.
- Decide the right documented kind for the two undocumented strings. `output-limit` (exit 7) looks
  right for the trace/envelope-limit failures; the overlay branch-ambiguity case needs an owner's
  judgement on whether `malformed-input` was the intent or a new documented kind is warranted. That
  judgement is a contract decision, which is why I am not making it unilaterally.
- Whichever way it lands, pin it with a test that asserts every `failure(...)` pair in pipeline.rs
  names a documented kind with that kind's documented exit. It fails on ten sites today.

Evidence revision: main 333d04b. Whole suite there is 133 reports / 1266 passed / 0 failed / 10
ignored, so nothing here is a regression -- it is an untested invariant.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CORRECTION TO MY OWN FILING, and a scope expansion. I filed this at p3 on the grounds that every
mis-mapped site was unreachable by a user. That conclusion was based on scanning `src/pipeline.rs`
only, and it was wrong: `src/cli.rs` carries the same hazard in a different spelling, and its sites
ARE reachable. Raising to p2.

`src/cli.rs` maps domain errors to CLI failures with tuples of the shape `(<digits>u8, "<kind>")` --
108 of them. Seven name kinds that are not in the documented set, so `src/cli.rs:862` cannot find them
in `ErrorKind::ALL` and falls back to guessing a kind from the exit code, publishing that instead:

| kind raised | code | published to the caller as | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `missing-snapshot` | 10 | `invalid-provider-response` | **materially untrue** |
| `revision-conflict` | 11 | `cache-miss` | **materially untrue** |
| `event-not-found` | 2 | `invalid-usage` | imprecise |
| `ineligible-alternative` | 2 | `invalid-usage` | imprecise |
| `invalid-arguments` | 2 | `invalid-usage` | fine |
| `skill-not-found` | 2 | `invalid-usage` | imprecise |
| `serialization-failure` | 9 | `storage-failure` | borderline |

The two that matter:

1. `missing-snapshot` (src/cli.rs:1297) fires when the roster snapshot retained for an event cannot
   prove complete membership, so a name-keyed judgment cannot be resolved without risking the wrong
   skill. Local condition, no provider involved. The caller is told
   `invalid-provider-response`, i.e. that Jev returned something invalid. **Reached by walking the
   documented adoption loop**: rank natively, observe, then `sr feedback <event> --skill <invocation
   name>`. Observed directly:

       {"decision":"unavailable","error":{"code":10,"kind":"invalid-provider-response",
        "message":"Roster snapshot missing or incomplete for event","retryable":false}}

   Recommended mapping: `incomplete-roster` (exit 5), which is already documented and describes exactly
   this. The hint should also name the two ways forward, as the sibling arm nine lines above already
   does ("supply the stable skill id"); the other is to rank with an explicit `--roster`.

2. `revision-conflict` (exit 11) is published as `cache-miss`. Exit 11 is documented as an
   offline/cache-only miss. A caller whose explicit feedback mutation lost its `--expected-version`
   check is told nothing was cached, and `retryable` then points it at a retry when what it needs is to
   re-read and rebase. There is no documented conflict kind, so this one genuinely needs an owner's
   decision rather than my guess; `storage-failure` (9) is the closest documented fit but loses the
   conflict/CAS meaning.

NOT A DEFECT, for the avoidance of doubt: the *refusal* underneath `missing-snapshot` is correct.
SilentFinch's comment in `resolve_event_skill_reference` states why better than I can -- "A retained
stable id proves membership even in a partial snapshot. A name needs complete membership: an omitted
skill may share it." And it does not over-reach: `if is_candidate > 0 { return Ok(...) }` returns before
any snapshot lookup, so README line 371's documented `--skill SKILL_ID` usage is unaffected. Only the
label is wrong.

WHAT LANDED. The guard test now scans both `src/pipeline.rs` and `src/cli.rs` and ratchets both
undocumented sets (9 pipeline sites, 7 cli kinds), so a new one cannot appear quietly and closing either
gap makes the ratchet fail and be deleted. The one true code/kind mismatch (`ambiguous-session` exiting
2 where the table says 3) is fixed. I am still not choosing replacement kinds, because that edits
docs/output-contract.md and AGENTS.md's exit list, and the two recommendations above are for whoever
owns that contract.

HOW I FOUND IT, since the method is the transferable part: independently reviewing a peer's change to a
fixture precondition in one of my own tests. "It fails without your setup change" was not enough to tell
me whether the limitation was in the fixture or the product, so I patched the assertion to print what sr
actually said on stdout. The mislabel was sitting in that output. Reading the diff would never have
shown it.

title: sr observe reads the transcript from byte 0 every pass, so a long session is never observed past the first window
description:
FOUND 2026-09-21 (RoseCoyote) while implementing sr-an94, by reading the ingestion path rather than by
running it. Evidence is code-level and is stated as such; the empirical case is listed below as required
before this is claimed fixed.

WHAT THE CODE DOES.
- src/cli.rs:1425 calls snapshot_jsonl(&invocation, &cx, &transcript_path, None, CursorKind::Observation).
  The fourth argument is the PREVIOUS cursor and it is hardcoded None.
- src/context/jsonl.rs, with previous = None, takes the branch `CursorKind::Observation => (0, rebuilt,
  false)`: the read starts at byte 0.
- The window is then bounded by OBSERVATION_DELTA_BYTES (8 MiB) and by record_cap() =
  NATIVE_TRANSCRIPT_TAIL_RECORDS (2,000 records), whichever binds first.
- The CLI still READS the stored ledger cursor for the generation CAS and still WRITES the watermark
  forward. So the cursor is maintained and simply never used to position the read.

CONSEQUENCE. For any session whose transcript exceeds 2,000 records or 8 MiB, every `sr observe` pass
re-reads the SAME leading window and can never see anything after it. Not "eventually catches up" --
never, because the start offset does not depend on the watermark. Skill loads in the later part of a long
session are therefore never recorded at all, and `sr stats` reports adoption from a prefix of the session
while presenting it as the session's figures. Sessions long enough for skill advice to matter are exactly
the ones this loses.

A second signal is computed and dropped on the floor: JsonlSnapshot.unread_backlog is set when the window
did not reach the end of the file (jsonl.rs:219 and :375, the latter also folding in hit_record_cap), and
nothing in src/cli.rs reads it. So the partial coverage is not merely unfixed, it is unreported, which
AGENTS.md forbids directly: "Validate before allocation and expose truncation/partial coverage", and
"Stats report adoption and operational metrics with denominators and unknown counts".

WHY THIS IS NOT sr-an94. sr-an94 is about a pair whose two halves are read by different passes; its fix is
a monotone attempted -> loaded upgrade in the write, and it lands separately. This is about a window that
never advances. They interact, though, in a way that must not be lost:

  sr-an94's upgrade is reachable TODAY only because the read starts at 0 and therefore re-reads the
  invocation. Whoever fixes this bead MUST, in the same change, rewind a bounded overlap behind the
  cursor -- large enough to hold a few maximal records (one record is bounded at 256 KiB) -- or a pair
  straddling the boundary becomes unrepairable again and sr-an94 silently regresses with no failing test.
  A note to this effect is in the code at the upgrade site.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE FIX. snapshot_jsonl validates a previous cursor with
`cursor.parser_version == PARSER_VERSION && cursor.identity == identity && cursor.kind == kind &&
snapshot_len >= cursor.byte_offset`, where identity is the transcript's (st_dev, st_ino). The ledger's
session_cursors row stores transcript_generation, last_complete_event_id and last_offset_bytes -- and NOT
dev/ino or the parser version. So a JsonlCursor cannot be reconstructed from what is persisted, and a
fabricated one would defeat exactly the replacement/truncation detection the field exists for. That is
very likely why the call passes None: the plumbing was not finishable without a schema decision, and the
None was left in place.

SO THE DECISION THIS BEAD OWNS is how to persist enough identity to honour a cursor safely. Options, with
the tradeoffs I can see:
  (a) Persist dev/ino and the parser version alongside the cursor. Exact, matches the existing check, and
      needs a versioned migration (observations/session_cursors are STRICT tables; ledger schema target is
      currently 2, so this would be v2 -> v3).
  (b) Re-validate by content instead of identity: seek to last_offset_bytes, read the record that ends
      there, and require its event id to equal last_complete_event_id. No schema change, one extra read,
      and it detects replacement and truncation for the case that matters. Weaker than dev/ino against a
      same-length rewrite that preserves that record.
  (c) Keep reading from 0 but iterate until the backlog is drained within the invocation deadline. Honest
      but O(session) per pass and still bounded by the deadline, so it does not actually guarantee
      progress on a very long session.
My inclination is (b) with the overlap rewind, because it fixes the defect without a migration and the
residual risk is a rewrite that preserves the boundary record's id at the same offset. But this is the
decision, not a foregone conclusion, and (a) is the rigorous answer if a migration is acceptable anyway.

TESTS REQUIRED, and the first is the planted negative.
- A transcript of 2,050 records whose Skill tool_use and tool_result sit at records 2,040-2,041: two
  `sr observe` passes record NO observation today. After the fix the load is observed. This must be run
  against the built binary, not asserted from the library, because the defect is in the CLI's call.
- A library-level case that snapshot_jsonl with a valid previous cursor starts its window BEFORE that
  cursor by the overlap and still excludes records further back, on a file large enough for the overlap to
  bind (> 1 MiB).
- unread_backlog surfaced in `sr observe`'s output when the window did not reach the end of file, with a
  test reading the JSON, so partial coverage is visible rather than implied.
- A replaced or truncated transcript still forces a rebuilt read rather than trusting a stale offset,
  whichever validation option is chosen.
- Repeated passes over a long transcript converge: pass N+1 starts after pass N's watermark, and the total
  bytes read per pass stays within OBSERVATION_DELTA_BYTES including the overlap.

RELATIONSHIP. sr-roadmap-l1i.6.26 owns "cursor CAS replay without skips" and is about not advancing the
watermark across unread bytes. This is the mirror image: the watermark advances honestly and is then
ignored by the reader. sr-roadmap-l1i.6.13 consumes the counts this starves. sr-an94 shares the symptom
(adoption reads low) and has a different cause.
close_reason: Independently verified (FuchsiaCave; RoseCoyote's half e4091d9+d7bf477 was previously unreviewed; PurpleFrog's e368b77 was verified by RoseCoyote) at origin/main bef5ebc. Required tests: (1) binary planted negative ledger_attempt_recording::a_skill_load_past_the_first_observation_window_is_eventually_observed; (2) library overlap >1 MiB: it was MISSING, so I added jsonl_snapshot::a_resumed_observation_window_rewinds_exactly_the_bounded_overlap (2850453; o39 is re-read, o00 is excluded, re-read count <= ceil(1 MiB / record), not rebuilt, appended records delivered); (3) unread_backlog in observe JSON (cli.rs:1859; asserted by both binary cases); (4) replaced/truncated rebuilds: a_rewritten_transcript_is_re_read_instead_of_resumed_at_a_stale_offset, truncation_rebuilds_instead_of_skipping_unread_bytes, replacement_rebuilds_on_new_file_identity; (5) convergence within the byte bound: the overlap is taken inside the same OBSERVATION_DELTA_BYTES read (read_window's to_read = min(available, cap) from the rewound start), and a_small_record_pair_across_the_observation_boundary_is_repaired converges at 1,999 and 3,999 within six passes. Option (b), content-proven resume, was chosen: no migration, and the residual risk is as stated in the bead.

comments.author: RoseCoyote
comments.text:
EMPIRICALLY CONFIRMED with the installed binary. The bead was filed from code reading; this is the run.

METHOD. Two transcripts generated by one script, differing ONLY in where a Skill tool_use and its
tool_result sit. Both are 2,050 Claude-native records in a workspace holding one skill ('alpha'), both
named <sessionId>.jsonl with sessionId and cwd on every record, both with a freshly initialised ledger in
an owner-only tree, and both observed TWICE, the way a periodic `sr observe` runs.

RESULT.
  pair at record 10    -> observe #1 observations_recorded=1, #2 =1,
                          observations table: [('s_d45ef1da5d76bb68da194302b8ace026cd0db246f95e3f5c17e829a3fbf0b0b5', 'loaded')]
  pair at record 2,040 -> observe #1 observations_recorded=0, #2 =0,
                          observations table: []

Same script, same binary, same skill, same tool call. The only difference is position in the file. The
load past the window is not merely mis-stated as 'attempted' -- it does not exist. `sr stats` would report
zero adoption for a session in which the agent demonstrably loaded the skill.

AND IT IS SILENT. Both passes exited 0 and printed
  {"agent_branch":"main","cursor_generation":N,"last_event_id":"...","observations_recorded":0,
   "session_id":"1111...","status":"ok","workspace_root":"..."}
status "ok", no warning, no partial-coverage flag, although JsonlSnapshot.unread_backlog was necessarily
true. A reader cannot distinguish "the agent loaded nothing" from "we stopped reading before the part
where it did".

The 2,000-record cap binds well before the 8 MiB one for ordinary transcripts: these records are small, so
the file was about 0.9 MiB and the record cap alone lost the tail.

HARNESS NOTES for whoever picks this up, since three of my four early attempts failed on fixture shape and
not on the defect:
- The transcript must be named <sessionId>.jsonl and its head records must carry "cwd" equal to the
  workspace and "sessionId" equal to the file stem, or observe exits 3 "Durable session identity is

comments.author: RoseCoyote
comments.text:
IMPLEMENTED, verification in flight. Recording the design and the decision I took, since this bead posed
three options and I picked one.

CHOSE OPTION (b), content re-validation, plus the overlap rewind this bead's cross-note required. Not (a),
persisting (dev, ino) via a v2 -> v3 migration, and not (c), draining the backlog inside one invocation.

  Why not (a): it is the rigorous answer, and it costs a schema migration on a STRICT table for a defect
  that content validation closes. If a future change needs inode identity for something else, (a) becomes
  worth it; on its own it is not.
  Why not (c): it cannot guarantee progress. Draining a long session inside one invocation is bounded by
  the 3,000 ms deadline, so a transcript long enough would never finish, and the failure mode would be the
  same silent undercount with more work done.

WHAT LANDED, three parts that only work together.
  1. src/context/jsonl.rs: an honoured cursor for CursorKind::Observation starts the window at
     byte_offset - OBSERVATION_REPAIR_OVERLAP_BYTES (1 MiB), with align_to_record so the first partial
     record is skipped. Ranking reads are untouched.
  2. Same file: a resumed observation read PROVES the watermark by content. The record named by
     last_complete_event_id must be inside the window; if it is absent the transcript was replaced,
     rewritten or compacted, so the read falls back to byte 0 and the generation advances. This is what
     makes it legitimate for the CLI to supply the current file's identity: the inode check becomes a
     formality and the content check does the real work.
  3. src/cli.rs: the stored cursor is actually passed, and `unread_backlog` -- computed by the reader and
     previously read by nothing -- is reported in the JSON and in the human line.

THE OVERLAP IS THE PENDING STATE, which answers what this bead and sr-an94 both asked for without any new
storage: nothing is retained between passes, so the 1 MiB rewind is simultaneously the repair window and
the expiry. A pair separated by more than that keeps its `attempted` row, which undercounts rather than
invents. One record is bounded at 256 KiB, so the window holds several maximal records, and it is charged
against the same OBSERVATION_DELTA_BYTES budget as the new bytes -- the bound this bead asked to be
explicit about.

ONE RESIDUE, stated rather than buried. The cursor namespace needs an agent branch before the context has
been parsed, so the resume uses the explicit --branch or "main". A native Claude transcript carries no
branch id of its own, so that matches in practice; where it does not, the lookup misses, the read starts at
the beginning, and behaviour is exactly what it was before this commit. Never a wrong resume, only a missed
one. Closing that residue properly means either resolving the branch before the read (two passes over the
file) or keying the cursor differently, and neither is worth it for a case I cannot construct with a real
Claude transcript.

TESTS, both driving the built binary against a ~2,100-record transcript with 600 bytes of padding per
record so the file exceeds the 1 MiB rewind and the load sits past the first window:
  - a_skill_load_past_the_first_observation_window_is_eventually_observed: repeated passes must CONVERGE on
    the load, and some pass must have reported unread_backlog. Convergence is the property that matters;
    asserting a single pass would pin an implementation detail.
  - a_rewritten_transcript_is_re_read_instead_of_resumed_at_a_stale_offset: rewrite the file under the same
    path with entirely different records and require the load in the new content to be observed.
Planted negative is the pre-fix behaviour I already measured on the installed binary: pair at record 2,040,
two passes, zero rows, exit 0. I will re-run it against this tree before claiming the tests detect it.

comments.author: RoseCoyote
comments.text:
THE WHOLE-SUITE FIGURE I OWED, and it found a regression in my own fix. Repaired in d7bf477.

THE RUN: 133 reports | 1,262 passed | 1 FAILED | 10 ignored, local `cargo test --locked --no-fail-fast`
at main's content. The single failure:

    tests/native_identity.rs::rejected_records_share_the_record_budget_and_leave_a_resumable_cursor
    assertion `left == right` failed
      left: 2000
     right: 100

WHAT I BROKE. That test builds 2,100 two-byte records followed by one good record, reads once, then
resumes from the returned cursor and expects the second read to skip the remaining 100 rejects and
yield the good record. With e4091d9's 1 MiB rewind the second read restarted at byte 0 — the rewind
saturates there — and because a window is bounded by RECORDS as well as by bytes, the entire 2,000
record budget went on re-reading rejects. The window ended exactly where it started and the good
record was never reached. That is the non-advancing window sr-jgez exists to fix, reintroduced by its
own repair, on a transcript shape I had not considered.

Why my own tests missed it: I padded each record with 600 bytes precisely so the file would exceed the
rewind. That made my cases exercise the path I was thinking about and blinded them to the one I was
not. A suite someone else wrote for a different purpose caught it, which is the argument for running
the whole thing rather than the subset you believe is affected.

THE FIX (d7bf477): if a rewound window ends at or before the watermark it resumed from, the read is
redone from the watermark with no rewind. The repair window is worth having only while it is free;
progress is not negotiable.

AND MY FIRST ATTEMPT AT THAT FIX DID NOTHING, which is worth recording because the failure mode was
invisible. I wrote the guard with a `start > 0` condition copied from the content-validation guard
above it — but when the rewind saturates at the beginning of the file, `start` IS zero, so the guard
excluded the only case it existed for. The test failed identically twice; that is what told me the
second run was not a flake rather than that my fix was wrong.

EVIDENCE AT d7bf477: native_identity 11/0 (the failing suite), ledger_attempt_recording 14/0,
jsonl_snapshot 11/0, observation_contract 19/0. The 133-report run above predates the fix and is the
reason for it; a fresh whole-suite run on top of d7bf477 is the next thing I owe here, and I will post
it rather than assume.

This also settles the debt I recorded when pushing e4091d9: the gate I said was outstanding has now
run, and it did not agree with me.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Confirming PurpleFrog's independent negative against MY fix, and agreeing it blocks closure.

Their finding: at a6f1ff0, a Skill invocation at record 2000 with its result at record 2001 stays
`[attempted]` instead of reaching `[loaded]` after six real `sr observe` CLI passes. That is a defect
in `d7bf477`, which is mine, and it was found by driving the CLI rather than by reading the diff.

Cause, which I accept in full. The progress fallback I added to `src/context/jsonl.rs` fires when the
observation window would otherwise fail to advance, and it buys that progress by dropping
`OBSERVATION_REPAIR_OVERLAP_BYTES` entirely:

    if kind == CursorKind::Observation && !rebuilt
        && let Some(cursor) = previous
        && cursor.byte_offset > 0
        && snapshot.cursor.byte_offset <= cursor.byte_offset
    { /* re-read from cursor.byte_offset with NO rewind */ }

The dropped overlap is exactly what a pair straddling the boundary needs: the invocation falls below
the new start and the result lands above it, so association never sees both. I traded a straddling
pair for progress without noticing I was making that trade. My own tests did not catch it because both
of the cases I wrote put the pair well inside one window.

Why I over-corrected, recorded because it constrains the repair: the ORIGINAL sr-jgez failure was not
about bytes. `native_identity::rejected_records_share_the_record_budget_and_leave_a_resumable_cursor`
failed `left: 2000, right: 100` because the 1 MiB rewind saturates at byte 0 on small records and the
`NATIVE_TRANSCRIPT_TAIL_RECORDS` budget is then wholly consumed by re-read history, so the window stops
advancing in RECORDS while looking healthy in bytes. So the property any repair must keep is that net
new records per pass is bounded below, not just net new bytes. PurpleFrog's proposed half-record-budget
overlap satisfies that by construction and is strictly better than my all-or-nothing choice.

Two cases worth pinning so the two failure directions cannot be traded for each other again:
1. Small records, rewind saturating at byte 0, budget consumed by history -- the original
   `left: 2000, right: 100` shape. The window must still advance.
2. The boundary pair: invocation at the last in-budget record, result in the next pass. It must reach
   `loaded`. PurpleFrog's negative already encodes this one.

PurpleFrog holds `src/context/jsonl.rs` and is implementing the repair; I am not duplicating it or
touching that file while they have it. When they post it I will verify as independent verifier, which
stays honest because the repair will be theirs even though the bead and the defect are mine.

This bead stays open. The earlier "implemented at e4091d9 + d7bf477, awaiting independent
verification" comment should now be read as superseded on this point: the fix is incomplete, not
merely unverified.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Independent verification of e368b77, PurpleFrog's repair of the boundary defect they found in MY fix.
By RoseCoyote at main 0d6744a. I am independent of e368b77 specifically: the repair is theirs, even
though this bead and the defect it corrects are mine.

WHAT THE REPAIR DOES. `read_window` now takes an `overlap_watermark`, and for an observation window it
trims the front of the already-read buffer so that at most half the record budget is spent re-reading
history:

    let prefix_len = watermark.saturating_sub(window.start).min(buf.len() as u64) as usize;
    offset = buf[..prefix_len].iter().enumerate().rev()
        .filter(|(_, byte)| **byte == b'\n')
        .nth(window.kind.record_cap() / 2)
        .map_or(0, |(index, _)| index + 1);

Four things I checked in the source rather than taking on trust:

1. The budget it halves is the right one. `record_cap()` is `NATIVE_TRANSCRIPT_TAIL_RECORDS.max()`,
   2,000, so the overlap keeps at most 1,000 records and leaves at least 1,000 for new ones. Their test
   converging 4,100 records within six passes is consistent with that arithmetic.
2. `map_or(0, ...)` is the important default. When the history in the window is shorter than half the
   budget there are fewer than 1,000 newlines in the prefix, `nth` yields `None`, and offset stays 0 --
   so a small overlap is kept in full and only an oversized one is trimmed. The cheap case is not
   penalised.
3. `offset == 0 && window.align_to_record` is correct: after trimming, the new start is already
   immediately after a newline, so re-aligning would be wrong.
4. `truncated_history: window.start > 0 || offset > 0` correctly reports the trim as truncation
   instead of silently claiming complete history.
   It reads only bytes already inside the existing byte cap, so there is no second read and no new
   allocation, exactly as the comment claims.

TEETH, and this is the part that matters, because the two properties here can be traded for each other.
I withheld the watermark at the call site (passing `None`, the pre-repair behaviour) and ran both
directions:

    a_small_record_pair_across_the_observation_boundary_is_repaired ... FAILED
      assertion `left == right` failed: boundary pair at 1999 must converge to one successful observation
        left: ["attempted"]   right: ["loaded"]

    rejected_records_share_the_record_budget_and_leave_a_resumable_cursor ... ok

So the trim is necessary for the pairing property and is what makes their case pass. And the progress
property survives without the trim, which tells us something useful about the layering: forward progress
is still guaranteed by the no-rewind fallback I added in d7bf477, while pairing is guaranteed by their
trim. The two mechanisms are independent rather than one subsuming the other. `src/context/jsonl.rs`
was restored and verified byte-identical to origin/main afterwards.

ONE OBSERVATION FOR WHOEVER TOUCHES THIS NEXT, not a defect. My fallback is still in the file and still
drops all overlap when it fires. With the trim in place it should no longer fire in the small-record
case that motivated it, because the trim guarantees the window advances -- so the fallback is now a
dead-man's switch that trades pairing for progress only if something else has already gone wrong. That
layering is correct in my view (progress is not negotiable; pairing is best effort), but it is nowhere
written down, and a future reader could easily remove one of the two believing the other covers it. A
sentence at the fallback saying it is subordinate to the trim would save them.

SCOPE. This verifies e368b77 only. My own half of sr-jgez (e4091d9 + d7bf477) is still unverified by
anyone but its author, which is me, so this bead does not close on my say-so. PurpleFrog holds that
review.
